items.title: Does a Universal Basic Income Bring Long-Term Changes?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
For more than a year, The New York Times followed recipients of a universal basic income program who received $1,330 a month for an entire year. There were benefits, but also the everyday challenges of being poor, and turning their life around "did not turn out to be quite that simple." Across Silicon Valley, experimental guaranteed income programs have quietly taken off. Google began funding six different initiatives in 2022 as part of a $50 million donation to nonprofits in the San Francisco Bay Area, saying basic income could be a novel way to prevent homelessness in one of the nation's most expensive locations. Each program has hundreds of participants who receive around $1,000 a month, and academics study the results. State and federal tax laws limit the lengths of the programs and the payment amounts. The studies have found that most basic income programs improve short-term employment and mental health while reducing food insecurity. But while data from these efforts has been closely tracked, less is known about the individual journeys of participants... The Times ultimately shadowed three people... All of the program participants, including the ones The Times followed, were previously homeless and transitioning off a housing stipend that paid for a portion of their rent, and many received the payments on top of other social assistance like food stamps. The Times's findings mirrored the academic studies. For all three recipients, the instant benefits of basic income were clear: They had breathing room for groceries, rent and other expenses. But the success of the payments in another area — giving people more free time and opportunity in the long term — was mixed. "It's a lot to ask of someone to get their life together in 12 months, when a lot of these issues are structural or systemic," said Jennifer Loving, who runs Destination: Home, a nonprofit that administers basic income programs in Silicon Valley. "And the world around them isn't getting cheaper." One recipient began going to community college — but resorted to taking one class at a time while single parenting — and using their monthly payments to help support relatives. In fact, the article notes that a recent study of 3,000 universal basic income participants found that money spent supporting friends and family increased 26%, "the most of any category. That was more than the increases for food (6%) and child care (11%)." Another recipient used the time to get help at a community college to find a higher-paying job. And one recipient died — but his mother used what he'd saved to help put his brother through a drug rehab program.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Court Agrees with EFF: Utah's VPN Law Demands a Technical Impossibility
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"When state lawmakers attempt to rewrite how the internet works," argues an EFF blog post, "users rely on courts to recognize that laws can't make technical impossibilities a reality." "That's why we were happy to see that a court has blocked Utah's attempt to outlaw the privacy protections of Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)." In a win for digital rights, a federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction blocking Utah's SB 73, the state's draconian anti-VPN age verification law... Signed into law earlier this year, SB 73 attempted to regulate adult websites by requiring them to block VPN users or to identify the physical location of visitors using them or similar tools that mask their network traffic. It even went so far as to prohibit websites from offering instructions on how to use a VPN to bypass these checks. This made Utah, to EFF's knowledge, the first state in the nation to target the use of VPNs to avoid legally mandated age-verification gates. The Utah federal court halted enforcement of the law's VPN provisions last week, ruling that the law likely violates the U.S. Constitution's prohibition on passing laws that significantly burden businesses and people outside Utah's borders. SB 73 burdens the rights of all internet users outside of Utah because it requires adult websites to either know every visiting user's physical location, and then block those in Utah, or to verify every visitor's age just in case they might be in Utah. The law's "actual-location provision in practice requires an entity to perform age verification services for every user visiting its site from any location because the entity would violate the law if even one of those users happened to be obfuscating," the court wrote. The court essentially ruled that Utah has less-burdensome ways to prevent Utah minors from accessing adult websites than requiring all users in the world to comply with SB 73. EFF's position is that "forcing platforms to detect and block privacy-preserving tools undermines user privacy and security worldwide while demanding the impossible." But there's another problem, explained an EFF email this week. "Age verification laws that are predicated on users possessing identity documents exclude critical sections of populations. And this problem is global in nature: Millions of people lack government-issued identification or encounter regular challenges to obtaining or updating it...." Every site-blocking bill has the same rotten idea at their core: That enforcing copyrights requires building a censorship machine for websites into the architecture of the internet. This is, of course, a disaster for a free and open web. These proposals keep coming, but there is still no way to create a mechanism for blocking access to an entire website that does not invite both deliberate abuse and lots of collateral harm to free and lawful speech. EFF has declared this month "Opt Out October," and each day they're offering new guides on how to "stand our ground and take control over what happens with our data."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Blue Origin Announces $330M Upgrades to Rocket Facilities for 'Multiple Flights Per Week'
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin said Friday it plans to make extensive upgrades to its Florida launch facilities," reports CNBC, "with the goal of supporting multiple flights per week by the end of the decade." "The company will add two more launch and landing pads for New Glenn, its heavy-lift, partially reusable rocket." A $330 million expansion to its Rocket Park campus in Cape Canaveral, expected to be complete in the summer of 2027, will enable it to produce up to 150 upper stages of its New Glenn rocket annually, Blue Origin said in a blog post. "These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently," Ian Richardson, Blue Origin's senior vice president of operations, wrote in the post. "As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade...." Blue Origin said it's building a new customer integration facility with the U.S. Space Force at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station that will enable it to "prepare multiple missions at once" when it's up and running. Blue Origin has invested more than $3 billion in its infrastructure and facilities in Florida, which now spans more than 20 sites across the state's Brevard and Orange counties, with more than 5,000 employees, [Ian Richardson, Blue Origin's senior vice president of operations, wrote in the blog post]. The article notes it's part of "a flurry of investment" as SpaceX stops offering commercial rides on its Falcon 9, "with $92.5 billion invested in the commercial space sector in the first three quarters of 2026, according to a report this week by venture capital firm Space Capital." And it happens as Blue Origin, SpaceX and other rocket providers "are seeing increasing demand from companies and governments trying to deploy satellites into orbit." "Launching at a high cadence requires a connected system," says Blue Origin's blog post, "one that manufactures vehicles at scale, prepares customer payloads efficiently, supports reliable launch operations, and quickly returns reusable boosters to service. We are building that system here in Florida," and "laying the foundation for a future where access to space is more frequent, more reliable, and more affordable, for the benefit of Earth."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Linux Maintainers Can Now Submit AI-Generated Code Without Declaring It
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Linux maintainers "have ruled that people no longer have to declare their LLM usage," reports XDA Developers, "as Torvalds himself calls a ban on AI 'utterly stupid.'" The first part of this story comes via a message sent to the Linux mailing list. It announces one of the major changes decided during the Maintainers Summit on October 8, 2026, in Prague, Czechia, where submissions to the kernel no longer need to use the "Assisted-by" tag... meaning that people can submit AI-generated code without needing to declare it as such. In some correspondence regarding concern about this new disclosure removal, the creator of Linux, Linus Torvalds, made his thoughts known... [Torvalds] compares an AI ban to getting rid of text editors, as doing so would prove that someone could write a good commit message without making any mistakes. He then rounds off his argument by asking, "Do you not see how UTTERLY STUPID those kinds of rules would be?" and stating that he simply expects the people working on the Linux kernel to "understand what they are doing." Here's the last line of Torvalds' post. "Quite honestly, in my experience, the people I respect and call intelligent are not the ones that shy away from using new and interesting tools." In a related story, Torvalds says he's used AI to help him understand patches that were hard to follow. And this week Torvalds even posted an LLM-assisted patch, reports Tom's Hardware: The development branch purports to fix an old issue with massive cache contention when many CPUs are reading the same file — a scenario potentially encountered when using shared libraries, databases, and web servers. Several developers had already made attempts over the years at fixing the issue, all with varied results, none quite ideal as an all-encompassing solution... He's now posted his solution in a development branch, and claims that he's seen a 23x performance improvement in a dedicated synthetic benchmark, though he notes that actual real-world impact will be far less significant, as "no real load" will witness those figures. Torvalds used Anthropic's Claude Code, reports The New Stack, and "said the assistant wrote the implementation, tests, and initial documentation, and reviewed the code under his direction. He ran the benchmarks himself, despite having previously criticized developers for claiming AI writes 99% of their code." Tuesday Torvalds submitted a 10-patch series. "Reviewers have since identified a race condition and raised concerns about memory reclamation," adds The New Stack. "Torvalds has handed further development to Kiryl Shutsemau, a Linux kernel developer who previously worked on the same bottleneck."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Deno Acquired by Cloudflare, Will Work on Open Source Self-Hosting Platform for Applications
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Cloudflare has acquired Deno, the company behind the [server-side] JavaScript and TypeScript runtime created by Ryan Dahl, the inventor of Node.js," Forbes reported last week. But Deno "has no future at Cloudflare, which will maintain the runtime for another year before ending its development," writes The Register. "That's OK with Dahl. 'I am now of the opinion that if you're choosing Node.js for building servers, you're doing it wrong,' Dahl told The Register." It all started with his team's work on the platform Deno Deploy, "We wanted to make running applications as straightforward as possible," Dahl wrote on the official Deno blog. "But building and operating Deploy also showed us how much complexity remained underneath that developer experience. I wanted to simplify that layer, too." This led to celld. Building on the Cloudflare Workers programming model, celld lets developers build distributed applications from the start while making the system simple to operate. What excites me greatly is that the scaling is built into the programming model, rather than infrastructure each app has to assemble itself.... We want to make this programming model the default way to build servers, whether you run on Cloudflare's network or your own infrastructure. Joining also means choosing where to focus our effort... Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development. Deno Deploy will continue operating for six months before shutting down. We will provide migration support for paying customers moving to Cloudflare Workers. [Deno's JSR package registry for JavaScript and TypeScript] will continue operating, with its infrastructure moving to Cloudflare. Forbes argues that this acquisition of Deno "turns a long-standing objection to Cloudflare Workers, the claim that applications built on it cannot easily leave, into a selling point." For CIOs evaluating serverless and edge platforms, portability now has a concrete answer... Released in August, [celld] is a single Rust binary that runs Workers and Durable Objects across many machines, with object storage as its only external dependency. Operators run multiple celld instances against one storage bucket, and the software handles placement, routing and persistence. Dahl and Belder will now lead an effort to merge celld into workerd and make self-hosting a supported way to run Workers applications. With this, customers can build an application on Cloudflare's network and move it to a private data center without rewriting it. "With Deno, we improved the experience of writing JavaScript," Dahl argues on the Cloudflare blog, "but we didn't fundamentally change what developers had to assemble around the runtime. The bigger problems are around networked applications: distributing computation, coordinating state, data storage in general, and autoscaling to meet demand..." Could the programming model make partitioning across machines part of the design from the start? The solution clicked into focus when I read about Cloudflare's Durable Objects. It provided a very powerful abstraction: the distributed singleton with a SQLite database. Each Durable Object is like a small, individually addressable server with its own relational database. Its JavaScript execution is single-threaded (which is easy to reason about), it handles WebSockets, and its local SQLite database can be accessed synchronously. By building a chat application using one Durable Object per channel, you have sharded your data and WebSocket connections, and thus made your application scalable... What excites me is the leverage this model gives developers: compute, relational databases, queues, and real-time communication primitives designed for applications distributed across machines. Now Dahl and 12 of his Deno colleagues "will work to build out Cloudflare's Workers platform," explains The Register, "expanding it for potential open-source use. He feels this approach is the way to go." "Right now, every other server is really operating at the Linux VM layer. That is not what Cloudflare Workers are," he said... The ever-fickle Dahl first debuted Deno in 2018 as a rewrite of Node. The name 'Deno' is an anagram of Node, and it was Dahl's attempt to fix everything he felt he got wrong with Node — built-in fetch, a permission model, native TypeScript support et al. Sequoia backed Dahl's company for $21 million in 2022, and as of August, Deno amassed 400,000 monthly users. Nonetheless, Node's gravity proved too heavy for Deno to achieve escape velocity. "What we found over years of working on Deno is that you can't really deviate from Node.js very much," Dahl told The Register. "As we continued to try to get adoption for Deno, we found we had to essentially backpedal on some of the original promises and become more Node compatible over time, and that left us as a kind of an alternative Node.js implementation." Going forward, Cloudflare will supply Deno with bug fixes and security patches for the next year, while Dahl looks for a new home for the MIT-licensed open source project. Dahl's worked could bring "yet another revolutionary turn for server-side JavaScript," the article argues, "offering a runtime that would require only 300 KB of memory per instance, rather than the hundreds of megabytes now required for Node/Deno. Such savings could quickly add up for a cloud provider, especially one serving the voracious agentic market." And as Dahl wrote on the Deno blog, "The need for better abstractions is especially acute with AI. Durable Objects bring together capabilities that are particularly useful for agent harnesses: inexpensive, serverless execution, persistent state, WebSockets, and a high-level JavaScript interface. This is what I'm most excited to explore and why celld focuses on Durable Objects."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Personal Data for Millions of California Students Stolen in Massive Breach
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Millions of current and former students at California's public school have had their data stolen — including names, date of birth, and addresses — stolen in a breach, reports the Los Angeles Times. The breach affects students "who took the state's mandated standardized tests that annually assess their academic proficiency, education officials announced Friday." The compromised information affects many more than the state's current 5.7 million public-school students as the breach dates back to 2023 enrollments. Students who left California but did not confirm their transfer to another school also were affected, dating back to 2006. The data breach involved [nonprofit] Educational Testing Service or ETS, which provides extensive services to California [including test participation and assessment data]... Affected former students, including those who are now adults, are eligible for 24 months of free identity-protection services and identity-restoration help if there is identity theft. Officials said that parents and guardians may want to consider requesting a free credit freeze for their children who are under 16 to help prevent unauthorized accounts from being opened in the names of their children. The breach involved a compromised login credential, according to a web page about the incident from California's Department of Education. The compromised credential was then used to copy files with student information at "various" times between May 22 and September 18, 2026, which drew concern from a cybersecurity expert interviewed by the Los Angeles Times: "A stolen login credential should not become a months-long passport to millions of students' personal records," said Anton Dahbura, executive director of the Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute. "If that is what happened here, the critical question is why authentication safeguards, access restrictions, and monitoring systems failed to detect and stop the unauthorized activity." He added: "Incidents like this expose a fundamental weakness in how we manage student data: School systems may outsource the storage and processing of sensitive information, but they cannot outsource the consequences of a breach. When millions of student records are concentrated with a single vendor, one security failure can become a statewide problem with consequences that follow children for years." A spokesperson for ETS told the Times that they've now implemented additional safeguards, including strengthened access controls, enhanced monitoring, and more third-party review of their security practices.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Will New Documentary Make Theranos Founder Elizabeth Holmes More Sympathetic?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
TechCrunch writes: "Isn't it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like ... a business scam?" comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes. One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. "I never actually made that connection," says Holmes. "I think it's a pretty different situation...." We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can't figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos' blood-testing devices didn't work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Business Insider says the scariest thing about the new documentary "is how much I wanted to believe her." SFGate calls it "one of the finest works of journalism I've ever seen." As Fielder ingratiates himself with Holmes and [her husband] Evans, he gets them comfortable enough to ask the hard questions: about Theranos, about prison, and even about themselves. The resulting footage is often shocking. You will see Elizabeth Holmes, who still maintains she did nothing wrong, answer "no" when Fielder asks her if she's ever lied in her life... [Y]ou will also see Holmes and Evans spend a great deal of time in this movie attempting to boot up Theranos 2.0. They even go so far as to drag out some of the original Theranos blood testing apparatus, which looks like a bunch of random parts from TigerDirect they hooked together, to show Fielder what their product can do. We do not see it doing anything on screen, but the couple assures that it we would if it was, like, hooked up properly. These scenes are extremely funny, but funny isn't what Fielder is looking for. He's trying to figure out if this woman is a clueless naif, if she believes her own lies, or if she is playing the character of an innocent woman, and doing so with such effectiveness that, to paraphrase Fielder, she might be the most manipulative person in the world. The answer proves fabulously elusive, and so Fielder and Oppenheim go to extremes in their attempt to find it. They hold the camera on Holmes' rubbery elfin face for what feels like hours at a time, to see if she'll blink (figuratively or literally!). They interview Holmes' visiting parents, with the father, former Enron exec Christian Holmes, casually telling Fielder that everything changed for his daughter "when she was raped." To the furthest extreme, they bring in actress Amanda Seyfried — who played Holmes in the Hulu TV show "The Dropout" — to recreate any dialogues Fielder had with Holmes herself that couldn't be recorded on camera. Seyfried is so convincing in mimicking Holmes that you, the audience, might forget which scenes were Seyfried talking to the camera and not Holmes herself. I know I did. Continuing that theme in the film, TechCrunch notes, is how her husband Billy Evans "has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she's actually there." Elizabeth Holmes "comes off in the doc as every bit as innately bizarre as anyone showing up for a cinematic freak show might hope," writes Variety: My personal hunch is that Fielder came away thinking Holmes is on the level, to the extent that someone who sometimes seems like an AI program's idea of how a human should behave can be on the level. There are a few possibilities that might explain how Holmes comes off the way she does in the movie: (a) She is a simpleton. (b) She is a conniving sociopath who happens to be utterly brilliant at playing a simpleton. (c) Somewhere between those poles, she is the very emblem of a woman who throughout her life has put herself in the sway of controlling men, to the detriment of her intellect, willpower and emotional development... Is it possible that the more you learn about someone, the less you might know how to think about them? Meanwhile, NBC News recently reported: Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted of fraud for siphoning hundreds of millions of dollars from several high-profile investors, is scheduled to be transferred from a minimum-security federal prison to a halfway house next year, according to one of her victims... [America's Department of Justice "is required by law to notify victims of crime of case developments through letters and emails," the article points out.] She was sentenced in 2022 to 11 years and three months in prison. She and her business partner, Ramesh "Sunny" Balwani, were ordered to pay 12 victims a total of $452 million in restitution. Holmes has been serving that sentence at a minimum-security prison in Bryan, Texas. The halfway house will provide her greater freedom... In March, a judge cut Holmes' sentence from 135 months to 123 months. According to a court document, the judge agreed with Holmes that she did not personally cause "substantial financial hardship" to her victims. NBC News adds that a prison consultant they interviewed "said inmates who report to halfway houses can work, have phones, drive to religious services or shop for things they need and earn passes for weekends at home."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Scientists Discover Why Microplastics Trigger Inflammation
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Scientific American: Microplastics are a source of extreme concern for health: the presence of these tiny pieces of plastic has been linked to heart attacks, stroke, dementia and brain tumors. But what drives these associations is unclear. Now a study published in Nature offers a tantalizing clue: microplastics interact with water, generating highly reactive molecules. When microplastics come into contact with water, the water near their surface can become chemically active, generating highly reactive species that can modify nearby substances, including biologically important molecules. As plastics wear down to microscopic sizes, their surface-to-volume ratio increases dramatically. For example, when a credit card is fragmented into particles some 10 microns in diameter, there is a more than 200-fold increase in its surface area, says Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University and one of the senior authors of the study. As a result, any chemical activity is amplified. Min and his colleagues examined various microplastics -- including polystyrene, polyethylene, polyvinyl chloride, polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate. Plastic surfaces are hydrophobic, meaning they repel water, Min says. Thus, water molecules cannot form the hydrogen bonds they maintain in liquid form. That changes molecular arrangements, and, in turn, the change influences the local electrical environment and chemical reactivity. The presumed chemical inertness of bulk plastics overlooks the toxicity of their fragmented microscale forms. "For microplastics, this is especially important because fragmentation creates enormous amounts of new surface area," Min says. In past research, microplastics have been shown to cause inflammation, oxidative stress and decreased mitochondrial activity. The new study provides a possible mechanism for this, showing that plastic-water interfaces can perturb proteins, cell membranes, and more. How this might contribute to damage in living tissues in humans is still unclear, Min says. "Ultimately, we hope to connect fundamental interfacial chemistry with quantitative measurements of biological effects, which would help us better understand potential health risks," he adds.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: This Might Be the Earliest Known Spear Murder In Earth’s History
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that lived and died by the spear, drew unequal lots, paged Fox Mulder, and peered at an alien moon.

First, scientists discover a mortal spear wound in a Neanderthal who lived 75,000 years ago, possibly opening a window into the origins of hominid violence. Then: disparities from beyond the grave, an unexplained population of near-Earth objects, and the word from Jupiter’s moon Ganymede.

meets

Some 75,000 years ago, an adult Neanderthal died from a brutal strike to the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, and was subsequently laid to rest by their kin. 

Eons later, in 2020, the remains of this individual were unearthed from deep in the floor of Shanidar Cave, an ancient Neanderthal hangout in what is now Iraqi Kurdistan. The bones of the deceased, named Shanidar A, preserve the spear puncture in the shoulder blade, suggesting that they were impaled with the weapon through the heart to their back. 

Shanidar A—whose sex is unknown—also sustained a brutal face injury that had partially healed at their time of death, suggesting that this individual had been cared for while they recovered from this non-fatal wound. The body appears to have been carefully interred in a small area of the cave that contained other Neanderthal remains, implying it was an intentional burial ground.

“Shanidar A’s shoulder injury appears to have been fatal, but the apparent placement of the body in a location that subsequently became part of a tight cluster of Neanderthal individuals, who were likely intentionally deposited within living memory of each other, strongly suggests a level of care during and immediately after death,” said researchers led by Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge. 

Taken together, the discovery of Shanidar A adds to the evidence that Neanderthals nurtured each other in life and performed symbolic funerary rituals after death. These bones may also represent one of the earliest direct examples of interpersonal violence in any hominin, the term for humans and their close relatives, assuming that the Shanidar A was intentionally slain. 

However, it’s hard to distinguish whether the death blow was an attack from another Neanderthal—or perhaps a member of our own species —or if it was an accidental injury sustained while hunting.

Shanidar Cave was occupied by Neanderthals for at least 50,000 years leading up to their mysterious extinction. While we will never know the complexity of their stories, our human cousins were clearly capable of compassion, care, and respect for the dead.

For the past several years, researchers led by astronomer Beatriz Villarroel have discovered strange “transients”—unexplained objects or phenomena in space—in historical photographic plates from before the launch of the first spacecraft, Sputnik, in 1957. The nature of these transients has become hotly debated among astronomers, with theories ranging from instrumentation defects to lurking alien spaceships.

In a recent study, the team re-analyzed the transients with machine learning, an effort reinforced previous findings that “transient numbers diminish significantly in Earth’s shadow”—hinting they are real objects that reflect less sunlight in our planet’s shade—and that they are more likely within one day of atmospheric nuclear tests during the mid-20th century.  

“If one accepts that both key findings in this study represent real phenomena…we are left with a very small set of provocative hypotheses that would be considered highly implausible by most,” said researchers led by Stephen Bruehl of Vanderbilt University and co-authored by Villarroel. 

“For example, is it possible that unknown to the public there were multiple launches of artificial satellites long before Sputnik with some launches timed to coincide with U.S. nuclear tests? Or rather, do the current findings represent detection of a non-human technosignature? Finally, might our results represent detection of an entirely new yet unknown physical phenomenon?” 

“Additional research on this topic is clearly warranted,” the team concluded. 

Hard agree. When a mystery’s leading explanations include 1) secret satellites that upend spaceflight history, 2) ALIENS (!!!), and 3) exotic novel phenomena, it’s fair to keep digging for answers. My own preference is that it turns out to be some unholy combination of all three, but for now, we will have to just keep literally watching this space.

Inequality is in our bones

Let’s keep playing in haunted graveyards—it's spooky season, after all. This time, we’ll take a long walk through about 2,300 ancient burials in the Central Plain of China. In a new study, scientists probed the emergence of wealth inequalities in these ancient communities by studying this huge sample dating from 9,000 to 3,500 years ago. 

The team assessed the relative wealth of the deceased individuals with a number of proxies, including the value of grave goods buried with them, their physical health, and chemical clues about the quality of their diets, which can be preserved in bones. 

The results suggest that inequality was present in many of these communities long before the rise of an official state hierarchy, and that “no single pathway led to persistent inequality across early centers of social complexity,” according to the study. However, one clear correlation that emerged in the analysis was the association between violence and inequality, with the former exacerbating the latter.

“In the Central Plain…the emergence of violence signals a structural transformation” that suggests that “violence contributes to the amplification and structuring of inequality, although reverse or reciprocal dynamics cannot be excluded,” said researchers led by Dongdong Li of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

While the rise of organized states and kingdoms can accelerate wealth stratification, this study proves that humans are capable of pioneering local homegrown inequalities in myriad ways.

We’ll close with an update from Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system, which orbits Jupiter. As the only moon with its own magnetic field and a candidate in the search for alien life due to its subsurface ocean, Ganymede has long fascinated scientists.  

Now, a team has compiled comprehensive observations of Ganymede’s surface terrain using observations from a range of advanced telescopes, including the Very Large Telescope in Chile and the James Webb Space Telescope. The aim of the study, in part, is to prepare for two spacecraft currently en route to Jupiter—the European JUICE mission, and NASA’s Europa Clipper—which will arrive in the early 2030s. 

Ganymede “remains a cornerstone object of planetary science due to its geological complexity, internal magnetic field, and potential astrobiological interest based on the presence of a subsurface conducting ocean,” said researchers led by Clement Royer of Paris-Saclay University. “Its surface morphology…argues for a history of significant endogenic activity, possibly including plate-like tectonics and cryovolcanism.”

Indeed, one of Ganymede’s most interesting surface features is a mysterious “darkening agent" that extends over much of the moon’s equatorial regions. The composition of the darkening agent “remains unresolved,” according to the study, though likely guesses include carbon-rich graphite or iron-rich magnetite.

The team anticipates that the Jupiter-bound spacecraft “will provide an unprecedented view of the surfaces of the Jovian moons” that will reveal many of their secrets. At least that’s one thing we can look forward to from the 2030s.

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: Astronomers Discover the First Green Star
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Astronomers have identified what may be the first genuinely green star, a white dwarf called WD J1330+6435 located about 326 light-years from Earth. Space.com reports: The researchers found that some dead star white dwarfs can go a little green around the gills after snacking on orbiting planets. An example of this is WD J1330+6435, a cool white dwarf located around 326 light-years away, which has been accreting rocky material from a planetary companion. This has enriched its atmosphere with calcium, lithium, and sodium, and the team's model suggests this would have led WD J1330+6435 to adopt a green hue. [...] The researchers think that no other star, living or dead, has ever been credibly reported as green. That makes WD J1330+6435 the first known genuinely green star. "The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow," Hollands said. "Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star. It feels like something out of science fiction." The researchers also discovered what may be the reddest star ever observed, the white dwarf WD J1011+2845, located just 48 light-years away. The findings have been published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Over $600 Million In Polymarket Election Trades Took Place After Races Ended
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even "truth machines" offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories. Two global election markets on Polymarket's offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win. The report focuses on suspicious trading activity surrounding elections in Ethiopia and Romania, where researchers uncovered $284 million in questionable trades tied to Ethiopia's election and periods when 99.6% of trading volume in a Romanian election market was flagged as suspected "wash trading." According to Wired, "wash trading is a type of market manipulation in which accounts repeatedly buy and sell assets to create the illusion of heavy trading activity, when in reality, money is simply moving back and forth." Some accounts may also be artificially inflating their activity to qualify for potential cryptocurrency token rewards, a practice known as "activity farming." In response to the Ethiopian trading activity, Polymarket told Wired that the company "immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading." The company did not explain why the suspicious trades were allowed to continue for months before action was taken.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: MLB Plans To Play Stupid Games With Its Website Again In Upcoming Lockout
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
Back in the much simpler times of 2021, we wrote about some of the games Major League Baseball decided to play as part of a brief owner’s lockout of players while both sides negotiated a collective bargaining agreement. This included essentially scrubbing the MLB website of all pictures of current players, stories about current players, and other references to current players other than their names, current and career stats, and the teams they played for. The league claimed that this was all to comply with federal labor laws, but nobody seemed to think that made much sense. Instead, this looked like an attempt to punish members of the MLBPA by taking them out of the spotlight as much as possible. That ultimately backfired, with MLB players changing their social media profiles to the blank silhouette that appeared on MLB.com while they made fun of the entire effort. It all made the league look very petty and very stupid.

In addition to instructing teams on what they are allowed to speak with players about, as well as what conduct they are allowed to engage in if they attend the weddings of players (yes, seriously), the website will once again be transformed into a useless landing page filled with all the things the public doesn’t care about when it comes to baseball.

Additionally, the league’s website will once again remove videos and player images during a lockout, per The Athletic. That includes altering articles and headlines.

“Player images (including from their profile pages) and videos would be removed, and player names and pictures would be removed from article headlines.”

There will almost certainly be a lockout, which means this is likely to go into practice once again, unless the league reverses course. Which it absolutely should. This petty nonsense is not a needle-mover for public sentiment, which is half the game in a labor dispute in professional sports. The league is also on very shaky footing arguing they need a salary cap for competitive balance, given the last four teams in the playoffs that are currently going includes three teams that are small-salary teams compared with the rest of the league.

This is purely about MLB owners attempting to claw back money from the players who are actually performing on the field through artificial limits on spending. Spending that, by the by, is currently being done by those same owners who say they need to limit spending.

None of it makes much sense in the macro. And, for our purposes, it’s worth pointing out that trying to strong-arm the players’ union by playing petty games with the league website is pointless and self-defeating.

items.title: Video Game Reverse Engineering Community Shuts Down Because AI Has Made It Too Easy
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The collaborative reverse-engineering site decomp.dev is shutting down, with its administrator saying AI has made game decompilation so fast and accessible that the community's human-driven model has effectively broken down. "The administrator of the website said that it has become impossible to keep track of which projects are primarily human-led and which ones are done by AI," reports 404 Media. From the report: "Historically, matching decompilation has been a brutally difficult, time consuming task, on the scale of years for any moderately-sized game with a number of active contributors," the pseudonymous admin of decomp.dev, who goes by Encounter, wrote on the site. But recent frontier AI models like GPT-6-Astra have made it trivially easy to decompile a game: "They are significantly better at following complex directions, cross-referencing resources for symbols or debug information, and writing natural code with enough guidance," Encounter wrote. "It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way. What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Something Else To Look Forward To: AI Worms
items.author: Glyn Moody
items.content:
Back in the early days of the Internet – 1988 to be precise – the self-replicating computer program known as the Morris worm spread across the network and shut down thousands of online VAX and Sun computers. It was a good example of software going rogue, but doing exactly what its creator had intended it to do without understanding the consequences. As Wikipedia explains:

By instructing the worm to replicate itself regardless of a computer’s reported infection status, Morris transformed the worm from a potentially harmless intellectual and computing exercise into a viral denial-of-service attack.

Since that early botched experiment, intentionally malicious worms have been written to create botnets that can launch DDoS attacks, for example to overwhelm systems punitively, or for the purpose of blackmail. Examples include Mirai and the later Aisuru-Kimwolf. These worms targeted specific kinds of Internet-connected hardware. But the arrival of AI agents that can carry out actions autonomously brings with it a new threat: AI worms potentially able to seek out, hack into, and infect any device that is online. Researchers at Anthropic have been studying this possibility:

small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes….Unlike non-AI malware, [such a replicator] could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. 

artificial intelligence (AI) agents enable a fundamentally new threat: a worm that generates tailored attack strategies to each target it encounters. The worm parasitically uses compromised machines to run open-weight large language models (LLMs) to sustain its reasoning, or extend its reach for further attacks. Deployed on a network of machines spanning Linux, Windows, and IoT (Internet of Things) devices, the worm propagated by exploiting common, real-world corporate network vulnerabilities.

The Anthropic researchers explored whether an AI worm could run a capable model in a distributed fashion across low-power IoT devices, as “shards”:

A model that’s too large to fit on one device can be split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model [that is, an LLM that contains fewer than 30 billion parameters] include smart fridges, smart ovens, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers. A growing number of home and business devices, such as security cameras and video-conferencing units now ship with small built-in AI chips, designed to run AI models on the device itself.

A 26B model running across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes, costing around $55 each, created manually by the researchers as a demo system, showed that IoT devices could indeed run quite capable models as shards, albeit slowly – at 0.39 tokens per second. Building on that result, the research project sought to answer two questions:

First, can small models get a model running on unfamiliar hardware? And second, can they do the whole cycle (find an uninfected device, copy themselves over, start running there, and repeat) all together in a single run?

The answer to both is “yes” – details in the Anthropic paper. The good news is that the process is very slow, typically taking one or two days to replicate. As the researchers put it: “As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days.” However, they also caution that things will speed up as IoT hardware becomes more powerful, and LLMs more compact. They write in conclusion:

As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.

These replicators will not be an example of AI agents “going rogue”, but of humans intentionally exploiting new capabilities for malicious purposes – or perhaps simply releasing badly written software, just like the Morris worm all those years ago.

items.title: China's Tencent Says AI Agents Showed Unintended Browsing Behavior
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Tencent says AI agents used to evaluate third-party models engaged in unintended web-browsing behavior while trying to retrieve data from Alibaba's Amap service. The announcement marks a rare acknowledgment of "rogue" agent activity by a major Chinese tech company. Reuters reports: Tencent Hunyuan, the company's artificial intelligence unit, said in a post on X that the activity did not originate from its Hunyuan models. Its review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination, it said. The Swarmchasers researchers said the agents sought information such as the commonly used entrances at Chinese parks, museums and zoos. [...] Swarmchasers said it used the word "rogue" to describe agents taking actions outside their intended scope or completing a task in unintended ways. After routine automated requests were blocked, the agents tried other methods, including public web tools that could open pages and run code, routing requests through other websites and using Amap keys and security codes found in publicly available software code. Swarmchasers said it found no evidence that the agents breached Amap's main anti-bot safeguards. Most of the 2,818 attempts it recorded either failed or returned anti-bot pages, login screens or blank results. Some requests returned information through cached pages and intermediary services, including data on visitor arrivals at Chengdu Zoo, Swarmchasers said. The researchers said they could not determine whether an agent read the result or completed its task.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Steam For Linux Finally Goes 64-Bit
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Valve has released a new Steam Client beta that finally moves the Linux client to 64-bit architecture, while also placing it inside a containerized Steam Runtime environment. However, Linux users still need 32-bit libraries and graphics drivers for compatibility, meaning fully 64-bit-only systems remain unsupported. VideoCardz.com reports: Valve's updated requirements explicitly state that 64-bit-only installations are not supported. Systems must still provide both 32-bit and 64-bit libraries and graphics drivers, including multilib support. The new client also requires Linux kernel 5.6 or newer and glibc 2.31 or newer. The update also introduces Steam Achievement Sets, a feature we covered earlier that allows developers to organize achievements into separate groups for base games, DLCs and seasonal content. Players can complete individual sets without losing their existing completion status when developers add more achievements. Valve has also updated the achievements page to display progress across these groups. The 64-bit Linux client and Achievement Sets are currently available through the Steam Client Beta. Valve has not confirmed when these changes will reach the stable Linux release. Until then, users on the regular Steam client will continue using the existing architecture.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of the unethical and likely illegal acts its agents are performing.

The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale.

Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission

In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said. “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.”

items.title: Meta May Use Sweeping New Commercial TOS to Avoid Millions In AI Licensing Fees
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Meta is facing criticism over updated commercial terms taking effect October 30 that could give the company broad permission to scrape content from websites linked to business accounts and use it to train AI. Legal experts warn the changes could undermine lucrative AI licensing deals for news publishers, with no direct opt-out for businesses that accept the terms. Ars Technica reports: As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta's terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans. "While journalism isn't the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab," the lab said. [...] Notably, there is no mention of AI, but it's inferred from a single use of the word "train" and references to automated scraping and crawling. Meta's spokesperson told Nieman Lab that Meta has no plans to use the terms as a legal basis to ignore robots.txt instructions that block scraping on news sites. The company still allows news organizations to opt out of scraping and provides instructions on how to block crawling. A spokesperson told Ars that "there is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false." However, should courts affirm that AI training non-news articles is fair use, news organizations question if Meta's stance might change, and the terms could be used to freely grab access to content by legally overriding robots.txt instructions.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: An OpenAI Research Agent 'Stole' Test Ethereum to Finish a Coding Task
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An OpenAI research model reportedly accessed an Ethereum testnet wallet without permission in order to complete a coding task during internal training. "This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI wrote. Engadget reports: The incident, which occurred on June 26, happened while a GPT-5.6 Sol model was in internal training. The task involved updating a crypto trading prototype and deploying contracts (publishing special code) on an Ethereum test network called Sepolia. Payment of a network fee is required for such contracts, but OpenAI "supplied no funded wallet and gave no permission to spend funds from an account the model found independently," OpenAI said in the report. The lack of funds at first stymied the agent, but it was not to be discouraged. The model reasoned that it could use public developer recovery phrases (similar to those you might use to recover a password) to access keys from unauthorized accounts. It tracked down 362 addresses open to that avenue of attack and found one that held enough Sepolia ETH to finish its deployment (to be clear, Sepolia ETH has no value outside of testing). Like many criminals, the agent reasoned that someone must have left this access open for automated draining of the ETH "faucets." It also figured that the crypto was effectively "abandoned" and "valueless," according to OpenAI's misalignment records. The piece de resistance was that the agent "did not disclose that it had selected a funded account through a public recover phrase or spent that account's balance," OpenAI said. To prevent similar events in the future, the company is now monitoring all traffic and paging security if live internet access is detected.

items.title: 11 Or 13 Justices Start An Arms Race. 100 Justices Might Actually End It.
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
For years, the idea of expanding the Supreme Court has been dismissed as a fantasy among “serious” thinkers. However, with it becoming ever more clear that the Supreme Court has gone completely off the rails and is now a purely partisan entity, rather than one doing neutral adjudications, more people are open to the idea of “fixing” or “reforming” the court in some form or another. Plenty of reforms are regularly suggested, from term limits to strict ethics and abstention rules. But one that gets the most attention is expanding the court.

Part of this also has to involve a more balanced system for bringing the number of Justices up to 100 without it being initially overweighted with ideologically biased Justices to one side. The most obvious initial system is to elevate a bunch of existing appeals court judges (currently there are 179 such seats), but doing so in a manner that requires some form of bipartisan consensus (at least one Senator from each party?) to agree to the elevation. Yes, such a system risks deadlock, but if there’s broad agreement that the process won’t tilt the Court toward either side, there’s at least a path to making it work. We have seen something kind of like this work with the FTC and the FCC and their bipartisan commissioners — at least until Donald Trump blew that up and basically fired all Democratic Commissioners (minus the one still hanging on at the FCC, because she’s needed under the law to allow the FCC to operate). And, yes, this ideologically captured Supreme Court blessed Trump doing so, but that’s all the more reason to set up a stronger system to ensure a Supreme Court that can’t become ideologically captured.

This can easily be combined with a term limit structure, but I’m not convinced term limits make that big a difference under my plan, other than changing the political calculus of when to retire. And with 100 Justices, that calculus matters a lot less, because no single retirement can swing the Court.

I think this type of expansion deals with nearly all of the “negatives” people warn about when it comes to expanding the Supreme Court. Let me explain why, and then see how it holds up against Vladeck’s “hard questions.”

  1. By expanding to 100 Justices you massively dilute the power and importance of any single Justice. So much of the issue now is that each Justice has so much influence and power that every single one of them matters a massive amount. Each Justice individually has a strong likelihood of changing the way fundamental parts of America work, with effectively no true recourse. Expanding the pool to 100 Justices means that none are nearly as important.
  2. Expanding to 100 Justices, rather than the much more conservative suggestions of 11, 13, or even 21, likely defuses one of the first concerns people raise: that each party, whenever it takes control of Congress, will simply expand the Court again in its favor. I agree that that is a very real risk the expansion is just a few Justices. Then “packing” the Court becomes practical in some form. Leaping from nine to 100, with randomized nine-judge panels makes future packing much more difficult. It’s not impossible, but the much larger pool with the panel selection process makes it way more difficult to consistently bias decisions to the extreme level we see today. A smaller number makes it easier.
  3. Adding an en banc review process creates an additional check on consistent biases. En banc already exists in the appeals courts, and this could follow the Ninth Circuit’s model, where review goes not to the “full” court but to a larger, more randomized panel (the Ninth Circuit isn’t fully randomized, but the Supreme Court could be). Law professor Paul Collins has discussed the potential benefits of having cases handled by three-Justice panels at the Supreme Court with the possibility of alternative panel reversal, and many of his arguments for why that could limit extreme ideological capture would apply to my scenario as well.
  4. If this system were combined with term limits, and a better way to select the Justices that diminishes partisan bias, then it would limit a setup where one party could overwhelm the Court with too many Justices with a strong ideological bent, but rather would push for more Justices who can get support from both parties. I may have my own ideological biases, but any system designed to stock the Court with only Justices who believe in specific ideological beliefs will be seen as illegitimate. But a 100-Justice Supreme Court with an actual mix of Justices and beliefs is much harder to insist is ideologically biased towards either side, making it less a target of ideological capture.
  5. Side benefit: having way more Justices means they can handle way more cases more fairly, increasing access to justice for many parties who are effectively squeezed out of the Supreme Court by the heavy focus on so-called impact litigation, brought by parties seeking to use the Supreme Court as a tool to route around Congress. It might also help deal with Vladeck’s other big issue: the weird recent infatuation of the Court to make consequential decisions on the shadow docket with no reasoning.

I’m sure there are risks. But a massive shift in how the Court itself functions, rather than a small increase designed to swing the ideological balance, has a much better chance of surviving long-term without triggering partisan swings every few years. The goal of the 100-Justice system isn’t to swing the ideological balance. It’s to rethink how the Supreme Court functions to make it way more difficult for it to become ideologically captured in any way. And with such a big change, it also acts as a bit of a shock to the system, getting people to rethink the function of the court, to bring it back to being a true judicial body, rather than a political body.

Now, on to Vladeck’s “hard questions”:

  • How do we avoid touching off a race to the bottom, where each time one party controls the House, Senate, and presidency, it expands the Court to ensure an ideologically and politically sympathetic majority?

I think my explanation above gets at this point directly. Merely expanding the Court by two or four Justices likely does set off just such a “race to the bottom” for each time Congress switches hands. But by massively shifting the setup of the Court, greatly diminishing the importance of any single Justice, we can avoid the value of constant one-upping the previous party in control, and reset the judicial balance.

  • If a race to the bottom is unavoidable, how do we avoid further (and potentially fatal) erosion of public confidence in the Court—which will quite transparently be little more than a lever of power for whichever party last had such a trifecta?

First off, I think with my system, a race to the bottom is absolutely avoidable! And, again, there are other elements in my system that I think should increase public confidence in the Court. It diminishes the risk of ideological capture of the Court, it enables greater effectiveness and throughput of the Court, and includes a safety valve in the en banc system as well.

  • If eroding public confidence in the Court is a feature, and not a bug, how do we insulate against the same erosion of public confidence in lower federal courts?

Again, I think my plan doesn’t erode public confidence at all. If anything, it should rebuild it, by making the institution more resistant to ideological capture. It could also help restore trust in the lower federal courts because the Supreme Court itself should be more effective and able to take on more issues, which gives the lower courts more clarity, as opposed to the vague hand-waving we’ve gotten used to under Chief Justice Roberts.

  • What is the case for why expansion is a better way to achieve the desired reforms than alternatives that would (or, at least, should) avoid many of these forward-looking concerns?

Term limits by themselves seem to do very little to increase public confidence in the Courts. It still allows for ideological capture based on the party in power. Yes, it gets rid of a few very old cranks, but that’s a short term fix if they are just replaced by the next MAGA crank in line. A massive expansion with a push for some level of bipartisan consensus again seems like a much bigger lever towards resetting the Court.

The ethics enforcement system seems like it barely helps at the margins of the most corrupt scenarios, but does little more to help in other ways.

“Jurisdiction-stripping” would block the Court from hearing certain kinds of cases, but I’m not sure how that helps, other than potentially increasing the power of Congress in a way that could further unbalance our three branch system of government.

Vladeck also has suggested systems of increased accountability:

There are many examples, but these would include: (1) expanding the Court’s mandatory docket; (2) establishing an Article III Inspector General; (3) codifying existing standards (as opposed to raising the standards) for emergency relief; (4) increasing public congressional oversight of the Court (including of its budget); and (5) on a more basic level, heightening congressional engagement in the Court’s day-to-day work.

The paper linked above also includes specific docket reform proposals that… are… fine? But I’m not sure any really move the needle on institutional trust.

Finally, to Vladeck’s long-term focus on the shadow docket, I’d be open to a specific reform on that as well, requiring that the shadow docket be explicitly tied to actual emergency situations, designed to focus on keeping the status quo in such an emergency, and only up to the point when a full briefing/hearing process can lead to a full decision on the merits. That alone wouldn’t fix the Court’s reputation problem, but it would be a useful addition.

But, on the whole, part of the argument for switching to the 100-Justice system is the very fact that it’s not an incremental reform, but a rethinking of how the Supreme Court itself works in a way that shocks the system out of the mess it has currently become.

Just like no voting system is perfect, no system for selecting a Supreme Court will be perfect either. But I remain fairly convinced that a 100 Justice Supreme Court would be a big improvement over what we have today, and clearly better than almost all other suggested reforms, including (importantly) the much more narrow plans to increase the number of Justices by two or four, which would set off the very concerns Vladeck outlines in his questions.

items.title: CoreWeave's Debt Stress Tests Private Credit's AI Financing Boom
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: Private credit's expanding role in financing AI infrastructure faced one of its clearest market tests this week as CoreWeave's bonds fell to distressed levels, raising questions about how lenders are pricing a boom built on chips, data centers and customer contracts. CoreWeave has about $50 billion of debt, according to LSEG data, making it one of the largest borrowers linking private credit to the AI buildout. The cost of insuring its debt against default climbed to about 1,200 basis points this week, while yields on some of its bonds rose to roughly 15% to 16%, signaling sharply increased investor concern over its credit risk. "There is still a price. Investors are still comfortable financing it, but they're demanding more compensation for it," said James Martin, senior US credit strategist at SMBC, referring to projects further from completion. Carlyle estimates that private credit could finance roughly $1 trillion of the AI infrastructure buildout but warns that aggressive lending could create concentration risks similar to those seen in software lending. "The clearest lesson is not to avoid AI compute exposure, but to set concentration limits before the buildout accelerates further, not after," Carlyle said.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: DOJ Lawyers Starting To Get Hit With Sanctions, But So Far, It’s Barely Even A Wrist Slap
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
There’s been plenty of talk by judges about imposing sanctions on ICE and DOJ lawyers who have routinely violated court orders and constitutional rights, and straight up lied in court (or allowed agents and officers to lie in court). But not much has actually been done about this. So far, it’s mostly been threats of future punishment. But if there’s a sign of hope for the future, it’s this, even if “this” is a bit underwhelming. (h/t Kyle Cheney)

Sanctions are coming. Slowly. And almost comically. But it’s better than nothing, if only barely. A federal court in Arizona is finally going to “punish” an ICE lawyer for misconduct. The targeted wrist may barely feel the slap, but here it is, as delivered by federal judge Diane Humetewa in this recent court order [PDF].

The DOJ lawyer being hit with sanctions is Brooks Chupp, the Assistant US Attorney for the District of Arizona. Chupp is a Notre Dame graduate whose LinkedIn profile seems to have suddenly gone missing now that he’s been sanctioned by a federal court. According to his Notre Dame bio, Chupp served as a “research assistant” to Professor David Waddilove. It will surprise no one to know that Prof. Waddilove is a current contributor to The Federalist Society. (It will surprise everyone even less to learn that Waddilove claims to be a “legal historian,” despite apparently being far more focused on securing multiple degrees in “Theology.”)

That’s the background. This is how Chupp fucked up, leading to his being sanctioned by a federal court.

From the record here,the Court has little difficulty concluding that AUSA Chupp’s accusation against Petitioner’s counsel was factually baseless from an objective perspective. No evidence has been provided to support that Petitioner’s counsel “represented to ICE that Petitioner was not presently removable due to his pending motion before the Board of Immigration Appeals.” What evidence has been provided supports, at most, that Petitioner’s counsel informed the “El Paso field office” that Petitioner had an appeal pending with the BIA, but made no representation as to Petitioner’s removability. (Doc. 14-1 at 8). Objectively, there was no factual basis to assert that Petitioner’s counsel had “represented to ICE that Petitioner was not presently removable.”

This is not, as AUSA Chupp argues, an instance of “weak” evidence; it is an instance of no evidence. (Doc. 26 at 6). While AUSA Chupp may have desired to “preserve an argument based on an inference,” that inference was wholly unreasonable, unsupported by the evidence, and antithetical to the ethical rules that guide attorney conduct.

More simply put, AUSA Chupp lied to the court. Then he attempted to cover up his lies with factually unsupportable statements and inferences — things that are, of course, just more legally acceptable lies.

The court’s not going to put up with this, at least not from Brooks Chupp.

The Court has no difficulty concluding that AUSA Chupp’s accusation was, at the very least, negligent and possibly reckless. On its own this would be insufficient to justify finding a violation of Rule 11 here. Id. However, the Court further finds that the accusation was also frivolous.

Nor was the accusation here some minor or tangential fact, but was instead presented as a dispositive fact justifying Respondents’ continued detention of Petitioner and carrying with it the implication that Petitioner’s counsel had engaged in potentially criminal behavior. See 18 U.S.C. § 1001. As such, it required Petitioner to expend the effort and resources—in less than 24 hours—to secure a signed Declaration from his former counsel, complete with evidentiary support, and briefing in response. Only then, after that effort had been made, did AUSA Chupp “withdraw” the argument, and even then, only because he “d[id] not have specific records of what Petitioner’s attorney did or did not state.” Given these stakes and, as he himself recognizes, the “special role of AUSAs” (Doc. 26 at 2), the Court concludes—especially in light of how the accusation hardened from “unclear” on March 24 to “likely” on April 1 without any supportive evidence or reasonable investigation in the interim—that the accusation was both negligent and frivolous, and thus “tantamount to bad faith,” and, as such, in violation of Rule 11(b)(3).

So, what does this mean for this DOJ lawyer? Not a lot, unfortunately. I mean, he’ll be viewed as untrustworthy from now on (so expect a resignation or firing in the near future), but Chupp is only being ordered to spend a few hours being told things he already knows, but chose to ignore in hopes of pleasing the bloodthirsty bigots running/ruining the country at the moment.

The Court will therefore order that AUSA Chupp participate in at least one (1) hour each of continuing legal education on a) the special role of United States Attorneys and b) the need for evidentiary support for all factual contentions.

That’s it: two hours of CLE (Continuing Legal Education) that Chupp can likely apply to any outstanding CLE balance he might have racked up as a practicing attorney. As I said earlier, it better than nothing. But not because it’s something than nothing. On its own, it’s no deterrent at all. It practically suggests DOJ lawyers engage in lying and cheating because they’ll still have their jobs, their incomes, and their freedom, no matter how much they fuck with the legal system and fuck over people who just want their rights to be respected.

But it does do , although it will be some time before we see whether or not it will have any effect. It breaks the seal, so to speak. It signals to other judges dealing with similarly slimy DOJ lawyers that sanctions can be brought and enforced. Any judge hesitating to be the first to do these things in their own jurisdictions should draw some courage from this turn of events, especially if the Trump administration decides it’s not worth its time to step in every time one of its lawyers is caught fucking up. Hopefully, there will be more of this in the near future, but only better, faster, and harder.

items.title: Cops Used AI Generated Photos of a Child to Lure Out a Suspected Predator
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
Police arrested a Chicago area high school maintenance worker who attempted to meet a child for sex after investigators posed as a 15-year-old boy using AI generated images.

Christopher Thomas Mertens started talking to who he thought was a child through a dating app in September. According to written by the department’s FBI Task Force Officer McKailey Scott, the investigation was done by the Livonia Undercover Resistance to Exploitation Unit (LURE), which identifies and prosecutes child sex offenders. Scott set up an account on the queer-focused dating app Taimi with “an AI generated image of a teenage-appearing male with the name ‘Caleb,’ and no age listed on the profile.  

Scott wrote that an unknown user messaged “Caleb,” and they moved to Whatsapp. After a few minutes of talking, the man asked Caleb for their age, and when Scott — posing as Caleb — said he was 15, the man said “Im interested” and “Im hard now.” 

The investigator used a combination of tools, including checking the man’s phone number using Thomson Reuters CLEAR and running images of his face through Clearview AI to identify him as Mertens. For days, Caleb and Mertens exchanged sexually explicit text messages and Mertens made plans to drive to meet Caleb on his day off, believing Caleb’s (non-existent) parents weren’t home. Cops used Flock to look up and track Mertens’ car and see that he was driving to the meetup spot, but Mertens was also texting Caleb the entire time to let him know he was on the way and when he arrived. When he got out of the car, Livonia police took him into custody.

Two hours after being booked, Mertens told jail attendants that he wanted to speak to Scott. When Scott got to the jail, Mertens admitted everything, including that he works at a high school in Illinois. The complaint doesn’t mention which high school.

Investigators have been generating images of children for years. One of the earliest examples of these is Sweetie, a computer generated child developed by Dutch children’s rights organization Terre des Hommes in 2013 that the organization used to talk to men online. Today, police departments at the U.S. border use AI-generated online personas designed to interact with and monitor protestors and activists, according to documents obtained by 404 Media.

In August, a 24-year-old Connecticut man was arrested after soliciting an undercover police officer who used what “age regression technology” to appear as a 14 year old in videos. He was charged with enticing a minor and criminal attempt to commit risk of injury to a child. 

In 2025, a 45-year-old man after investigators used AI generated images of children to catch him distributing child sexual abuse material. He was recently to 12 years in federal prison.

And in 2024, the state of New Mexico after investigators set up a fake account, including AI generated images of children, that the platform allegedly recommended to “dangerous accounts, including ones named ‘child.rape’ and ‘pedo_lover10,’ in addition to others that are even more explicit,” the New Mexico Department of Justice.

AI generated child sexual abuse material is a for law enforcement. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has a massive rise in generative AI child abuse material, with criminals using it to extort and entice children, and children using it to other children.

Livonia police did not respond to a request for comment.
