items.title: How ChatGPT Targets Ads To You Based On Your Prompts, Phone Number, and Email
items.author: Joseph Cox
items.content:
OpenAI lets anyone inject ads into ChatGPT users’ sessions, targeting specific groups of people based on their email address, phone number, or a unique identifier on their phone, according to 404 Media’s own tests of ChatGPT’s advertising ecosystem.

While the ad targeting available in ChatGPT is somewhat standard practice across the advertising industry, the chatbot’s one billion monthly active users may not understand they, in some cases, are being specifically targeted because of their personal data the advertiser has uploaded to OpenAI. ChatGPT’s ad targeting is also novel in that it is also based on the prompts users enter into the chatbot, prompts that users may assume are private but which, as 404 Media has previously shown, may be reviewed by humans. Or in this case, used for ad targeting purposes.

items.title: Data Centers Are War Targets Now
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
In 2006, British economist Clive Humby “data is the new oil,” and big tech adopted the metaphor. Twenty years later, a dark side of the truism has been revealed. If the places where oil is refined are valuable targets in a war then so, too, are the places where data is refined. We’ve seen this not just in the Russia-Ukraine war, but also with Iran hitting Amazon Web Services data centers in Dubai in retaliation for America’s strikes on the country. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed strikes on Russian data centers and oil refineries and called them a “symmetrical response" to Russian aggression. Here we have oil and data together again, not as a metaphor in an economics lecture, but in the pronouncement of a world leader defending his country. conducting a war.

Three of Ukraine’s strikes hit data centers that belonged to Yandex, Russia’s Google-equivalent, and damaged the company’s supercomputers that housed some of its AI models. The latest attack hit a data center operated by Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank. It’s too early to tell what the effects of the strike on the Sberbank data center will be, but the three strikes on Yandex have disrupted internet and communications across Russia.

An online rumor said that the strikes on Yandex had the effect of taking down Russian bot farms, . The effects of the strikes on the civilian population were much more severe. Yandex is ubiquitous in Russia — it has its own app store, payment services, dating services, taxi and bus apps, and email services. The company operates six data centers in Russia and the strikes knocked two of them offline completely. People in Russia have lost access to their email, some of their data is seemingly gone, and taxi and bus apps only work intermittently.

ChrisO_wiki, an anonymous researcher who translates Russian social media posts for the western web, chronicled how the Yandex outages are hitting everyday Russians. “A taxi driver from Yekaterinburg says that after the service disruptions, he can no longer view his order history, and the status of trips is updated with a delay,” ChrisO_wiki said in a post on X and Bluesky. 

“The loss of Yandex's cloud services is also having severe impacts on Russian commercial logistics. Those who work with electronic document management are unable to register incoming goods, severely affecting manufacturers and distributors,” they .

Klaudia Klonowska, a who studies the effects of emerging technologies on international law, told 404 Media that attacks on data centers are so new that international law around them is still developing. “You have very limited situations in which they would actually qualify as lawful targets when they're used by the military, and even then, it's very difficult for the attackers to know whether that's happening or not,” Klonowska said.

If the data centers are purely processing military data, then they could be legitimate targets, according to Klonowska. But many, if not most, data centers are dual-use, meaning they house both civilian and military data. In many cases, disrupting daily life seems to be part of the point.

When Russia struck data centers in Ukraine in September, state-backed news agencies claimed it that supported Ukrainian intelligence efforts and was a lawful target. Ukraine denied the allegation. “So you see how difficult, because of the nature of these centers, it's really to pinpoint what is happening with them and who is using them and for what means,” Klonowska said. “Sometimes [Ukraine] mentions that these data centers contribute to Moscow's revenues that then fuel the war machine. But that's not enough to make them lawful targets. Retaliation is not enough under law.”

Klonowska noted that it is civilians who suffer most, not the military, when data centers go offline. “There are questions about proportionality given how widespread the attacks are,” she said. “A lack of internet access for very prolonged periods affects everything. It's all of the civilian services that are being disrupted, which you can imagine also includes things like hospitals, traffic, judicial services, etc. etc.” It’s worth noting that Russia has repeatedly attacked civilian targets in Ukraine, including apartment buildings, public transportation, .

According to Klonowska, international and humanitarian law needs to catch up with the issue and that scholars like herself are only just starting to understand the ramifications. “I think there's also another bigger question behind all of this,” she said. “Why have we gotten to the point where we have permitted militaries of various states to use civilian commercial data centers for their military purposes? By potentially using them and relying on them, they have opened them up to the possibility of becoming military targets.”

Disentangling civilian and military data probably won’t take data centers off the target list, but it will make international law more clear on which buildings are legitimate targets. It may also change how data centers processing military data are built. 

“France has recently announced that they have unveiled their underground data center on the outskirts of Paris that will be exclusively for military use,” Klonowska said. “Just as we expect them not to use schools or hospitals or other civilian residential areas to host weapons or other military equipment, we would, I think, increasingly need to mention this in the case of data centers.”

The idea that a data center might be a military target is not lost on the American communities facing construction of them in their backyards. America’s nuclear weapons scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) have partnered with the University of Michigan in an attempt to in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan. The people and government of the Township aren’t thrilled about it for a number of reasons and the city attorney has said that the data center would be a “high value target” in wars of the future. Los Alamos pushed back on this in a in September, around the same time Russia was striking data centers in Ukraine. LANL accused the township attorney of creating “that terminology without basis. It should not be interpreted as evidence of a known, specific, or imminent threat to the facility or the surrounding community,” the letter said. 

“Like other major research facilities, the center would employ appropriate security measures, including controlled access, cameras, and on-site security personnel,” it said. “Los Alamos and U-M would coordinate with local, state, and federal partners on matters related to safety and security.”

It’s easy to see where the people of Ypsilanti Township are coming from. When Ukraine struck three Yandex data centers in Russia over the weekend, its drones slipped past Russia’s air defenses. The idea that a town next to a data center, especially one with ties to America’s nuclear weapons programs, could sustain damage if the data center was ever attacked isn’t unfounded. The data centers smoldering in the world’s war zones proved that the township’s fears aren’t theoretical.

items.title: Starlink’s Entry Into Wireless Is Being Wildly Overhyped
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
One of the ways Musk fraudulently goosed SpaceX stock value during the IPO was by pretending that the company would very quickly (in just a year or two) grow from just 12 million global Starlink subscribers (just 4 million in the States) to something more akin to 300-500 million.

The way Starlink claims they’ll do this is by getting into traditional wireless phones and challenging incumbents like Verizon, though if you look at the actual details of the plan, it’s not well thought out.

Starlink wants to plunk down thousands of meshed femtocells installed on customer rooftops alongside existing LEO satellite dishes, something one telecom analyst recently stated was “one of the top three dumbest ideas in my four decades of being in this industry.” In part because the femtocells will eat up already dwindling capacity on the increasingly congested network (recall that Starlink customers in some areas already face “congestion fees” as high as $1500).

Musk Corp is also leveraging its cozy relationship with the Trump administration to hoover up as much spectrum as they can get their hands on. You might recall that Trump FCC boss Brendan Carr launched an “investigation” into Echostar to specifically help offload their spectrum to Musk. SpaceX also recently bought 14 megahertz of spectrum in the 800 MHz band from investment firm Grain Management, which bought the spectrum from T-Mobile earlier in 2026.

Starlink has even managed to pressure some Republicans into supporting broader cell phone unlocking rules, something the party has spent the last few decades helping entrenched telecom giants like AT&T and Verizon fight tooth and nail against.

The recent purchase was enough to send AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile stocks tumbling:

“Verizon closed down 8.75% on the news, its worst day since July 2002. Shares of T-Mobile dropped 13.27% while AT&T fell 9.81%, each notching their own worst days since 2013 and 2000, respectively.”

In contrast, the white supremacist’s space company’s stock only jumped around 1 percent for the day.

The problem for Musk is multifold. As Dish Network found when it failed utterly to disrupt the sector, it takes a lot more than spectrum hoarding and some greased palms to become a major player in wireless. Actually building a useful network the public wants to use that covers rural and urban markets alike is a massive cash sink investors despise in part because networks take years to finish.

The highway of telecom history is positively filled with the gravestones of companies that tried to cleverly out-maneuver giant incumbent telecoms, which are directly tethered to the heart of the Republican party (remember Starry?).

Space X and its boosters believe that simply having access to Starlink’s network of Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites is some kind of magic wand toward competing in wireless (they’re already partnering with T-Mobile for phone calls in out-of-the-way locations). But even normally staid telecom analysts have been shitting all over Musk’s femtocell plan, pointing out it’s not going to scale well:

“Given the laws-of-physics limitations, a Starlink network of small cells would probably have more holes in it than a hiker’s socks. Neither Lum nor Rhodes sees much likelihood of coverage in urban areas that enjoy mainstream and lower-cost alternatives. “It works best in rural because you’ve got fewer choices for fiber and so most customers are there. Where are your customers to repeat it in the city?” said Rhodes. “Well, they don’t exist because they’re not that stupid.”

There’s also the fact that Musk companies don’t really believe in customer service, and fail in most every instance where they’ve been forced to try. Both Starlink and Tesla Solar are routinely inundated with stories where customers can’t even get the companies to respond to phone calls or emails. Starlink also consistently isn’t particularly affordable for the folks most in need of access.

Starlink is (and will probably always be) a good niche broadband solution best suited for people out of reach of better, faster, more affordable options if they can afford it (rural homes, boats, RVs, wars, disasters). But Musk and Republicans have broadly tried to claim that the technology is some sort of magic bullet for connectivity. To the point where they redirected what ultimately will likely be billions of infrastructure bill taxpayer dollars away from faster fiber networks to Starlink.

The actual threat to giants like AT&T and Verizon is limited, though outlets like CBS buried that fact deep in their bullish reporting. Even a best case scenario requires a massive outlay of capital and a half a decade to even get close to begin trying to compete in the space, something SpaceX’s more reality-based investors definitely aren’t going to enjoy.

items.title: Mini Organs Launching to Space For Study On Aging
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Researchers from Mount Sinai, NASA, and Space Tango have launched miniature human hearts and brains to the International Space Station to study how microgravity and radiation affect organs and potentially accelerate aging. "If people are going to be living and working in space, then we need to understand what's going to happen to them," David Sachs, assistant professor of surgery at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. "But also, because it's interesting as a model of accelerated aging for studying people on Earth." From the report: The mini organs launched aboard commercial resupply mission CRS-35 on Tuesday morning from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. They are expected to arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday. The miniature organs offer researchers a unique opportunity to simulate aging in a much shorter period of time to understand disease and develop treatments. "Six months in space ... is equivalent to about 10 to 20 years of aging on Earth," Kevin Costa, associate professor of surgery at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. Sachs and Costa are sending up to 16 miniature hearts to the ISS to test how they respond to electrical signals and monitor how they may react to near-zero gravity. The technology, which is integrated into a miniature laboratory called CubeLab, was developed by Space Tango and simulates the natural environment in the human body. "[It is] slightly bigger than a shoebox, and it is a fully automated, miniaturized system," Gentry Barnett, chief technology officer at Space Tango, told ABC News. [...] As part of the new effort, the team is sending miniature brains, called miBrain, to the ISS. Around the size of a peppercorn, the miBrains reflect models of healthy and diseased brains. By exposing them to the space environment, scientists can see how mini-brains respond and better understand why living in space accelerates aging. Though the mini organs are not full-sized human organs, the researchers say they are good substitutes, cost-effective and don't take up much of the limited space aboard the space station. They also believe discoveries made in space can translate to uses in everyday medical care. The microgravity environment uniquely allows researchers to study what happens to humans with a sedentary lifestyle or prolonged bed rest, which isn't easily simulated on Earth, Sachs explained. "[The research is] translating to stuff in space, but it's also translating back to the research we do in the laboratory to help people with Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease," Joel Blanchard, associate professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine and neuroscience at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. Lisa Carnell, the director of the biological and physical sciences division at NASA, told ABC News that these experiments serve as a starting point for future research beyond low Earth orbit, including to the moon and beyond.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Schools Across US Protest FCC Plan That Could Disconnect Kids From Internet
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Schools and libraries from around the U.S. pleaded with the Federal Communications Commission to drop the idea of ending E-Rate, a $2 billion-a-year program that connects students and library visitors to the Internet. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has criticized school districts for having "experimented with a massive increase in screen time for students," and said E-Rate expanded too far beyond its original purpose of "supporting basic Internet access to schools and libraries for educational purposes." In June, Carr led a 2-1 vote to issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) seeking public comment on whether E-Rate should be "limited or sunset to reflect today's extensive connectivity rates." Carr's proposal could result in E-Rate cutting the discounts that schools and libraries receive for telecom services and equipment, and imposing more restrictions on how E-Rate money can be used. The FCC seeking comment on whether to sunset the program also raises the possibility that Carr might choose to axe E-Rate entirely. The National Association of Elementary School Principals told the FCC that it "strongly supports the continued operation of the E-Rate program and urges the Commission to reject proposals that would eliminate, substantially restrict, or impose new conditions on this essential source of connectivity assistance for schools and libraries." The Carr FCC already scaled E-Rate back last year by ending funding for schools and libraries to lend out Wi-Fi hotspots and for Wi-Fi service on school buses. "Importantly, the FCC does not have the authority to terminate the E-Rate program. The E-Rate program is mandated by Congress, and the FCC is responsible for administering it," the American Library Associated told the FCC. The American Library Association said "the FCC lacks the authority and expertise to regulate screen time or determine educational outcomes." In a filing, the group pointed out that under U.S. law, determinations about what content is inappropriate for children "shall be made by the school board, local educational agency, library, or other authority responsible for making the determination."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Epic Games Somehow Gets Even Worse On AI Than Tim Sweeney’s Anti-Disclosure Take
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
There have certainly been some bad takes on both sides of the AI in video games argument. In one corner, we have the never-AI-ers who reflexively claim that any use of any type of AI in any game is a total disqualifier. No quarter is given to nuance. No daylight is offered for discussion. It might as well be religion to those folks. Then, on the other side, you have people like Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney, who has not only directed his company to go all in on the use of generative AI in gaming, but actually had the chutzpah to suggest that his rival Steam’s inclusion of AI-use disclosures on its storefront are “irresponsible.”

But Epic has somehow gotten even worse on AI use than that. Rather than suggesting that generative AI is a potential tool for use in gaming, which can often mean its use is employed on the perimeter of game-creation, Epic has decided to make the use of AI compulsory.

According to a new report by Bloomberg, developers on the game were told to implement an “AI-first” production model using Anthropic’s Claude AI models. The team is not to use any more “hand-written code,” and even artists are being pushed to use the technology that has become a punching bag among actual players. The director of the unannounced game reportedly told developers that all art should be “generated with full AI workflows.”

“We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” Jake Jones, communications director at Epic Games, said in a statement.

It’s hard to overstate just how stupid this is. This isn’t handing artists new and interesting paintbrushes to use. It’s taking their paintbrush away entirely and telling the artists to simply tell a machine what to make. That is a terrible idea. It’s also completely antithetical to how other game makers have employed the use of AI. This is going to turn off both the public, which generally hates the idea of artistic interruption through the use of AI tools, and the pool of artists Epic does and could in the future employ.

AI models are getting better at coding, certainly. But what Epic is clearly doing is anti-artist for the sake of speed-running development after cutting human employment.

The upcoming shooter, which Bloomberg reports was supposed to release in March 2027, has now been delayed due to slow progress and understaffed teams. Despite a $1.5 billion investment by Disney in 2024 for collaborations that include this project, the Fortnite maker laid off 1,000 people earlier this year amid the battle royale’s struggles and the costs of ongoing antitrust litigation.

For the group that is dogmatically opposed to the use of AI in gaming, this is their boogeyman come to life. It’s the starkest example of bad corporate behavior enabled by AI that they could want. And it’s very hard to argue against them when there are bad CEOs and bad companies out here pulling this kind of garbage.

I won’t even try. I’ll repeat that I think there is a place for this technology as a tool to enable artists and enable more art. But if the gaming industry is too poisoned at this point to allow for that possibility to be employed responsibly, then so be it.

items.title: We’re Asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to End Warrantless ALPR Searches
items.author: Andrew Crocker
items.content:
Today, EFF joined the ACLU of Wisconsin in filing a petition to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, asking it to rule that the state’s constitution requires a warrant for retrospective searches of ALPR databases used by law enforcement in four cities: Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha, and Green Bay. We represent a religious organization, the Wisconsin Council of Churches, as well as an individual pastor in Green Bay.

As the petition explains:

Right now, Automated License Plate Readers (“ALPRs”) are recording the movements of vast numbers of Wisconsin drivers as they seek medical care, attend 12-step recovery meetings, attend religious services, participate in protests, attend political meetings, and engage in many other private, sensitive activities. Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology.

We all deserve to be free of warrantless mass surveillance. We all deserve to live in a country where surveillance vendors cannot help police upend our system of individualized suspicion. Religious organizations and officials like our clients have a heightened interest in protecting their location privacy because of the range of expressive associations their work entails, including facilitating gatherings for religious worship, as well as offering pastoral care, confidential counseling, and community support. Likewise, the people who visit houses of worship have a strong right to privacy against police monitoring of when they pray, seek addiction counseling, or attend a domestic violence survivor meeting.

This is our second lawsuit challenging warrantless ALPR searches, following Earlier this month, a federal court in Oklahoma became the first to rule that ALPRs are a “type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” and suppress evidence from a warrantless ALPR search. We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will agree.

Read the Wisconsin Supreme Court petition

items.title: Eight US States Sue OpenAI, Claiming ChatGPT Harms Young Users
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Eight US states, including Kansas, Arizona, and Montana, have sued OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT encourages children to harm themselves. The states are seeking changes to how the company's products interact with young users and the forfeiture of profits generated from their activity. Reuters reports: Attorneys general from the states, which include Iowa, Kansas and Arizona, filed the lawsuits independently in state courts, claiming ChatGPT is designed to be agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users. But the chatbot reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behavior and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings, the lawsuits claim. The lawsuits represent the most significant coordinated state action against an artificial intelligence company, adding to a wave of legal challenges OpenAI faces as it prepares for a public listing. Florida's attorney general filed the first such state suit in June. The lawsuits accuse the company of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about the safety of ChatGPT. The states also allege that the company created a public nuisance by endangering the health of their residents. The lawsuits seek orders forcing OpenAI to make changes to how ChatGPT works. Among other things, the states want the company barred from developing AI models that can improve themselves unless it can ensure those models are aligned with human values. The states ... are also seeking civil monetary penalties for OpenAI's violations of state law as well as damages.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Will Universities Respond To The AI Moment?
items.author: Kevin Frazier, Juliana Schroeder, Brian Frye, Nathanael Fast, and Rob Greer
items.content:
A key role universities play in society is providing knowledge that can guide public action. Moreover, public universities have a legal duty to serve the public. We expect researchers in universities to  produce and disseminate knowledge that can ultimately advance human flourishing and meet the informational needs of lawmakers, civil society, and the public generally. Yet too many schools are currently failing to meet this expectation in key domains. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT sparked humanity’s most pressing technological moment, many public stakeholders are left with more questions than answers about how to navigate this AI moment. 

Universities have only just begun to enable scholars and students to contribute to the massive task of providing adequate knowledge to guide societal action with respect to AI. This delay–perhaps forgivable for a brief period of time given that universities will never move at the speed of startups–is eroding the capacity and, as a result, legitimacy of these critical institutions. The longer that universities operate as if society were not undergoing fundamental change, the faster that faculty members will depart for other opportunities (e.g., in industry), potential and current students will opt for alternative paths to education, and stakeholders will decrease or even withhold ongoing financial support. 

Other individuals and more nimble organizations have rushed to fill the informational vacuum. AI labs, research institutes, and partisan entities now play a heavy role in shaping how the public and elected officials think about this moment. However, these parties–no matter how well-intentioned–have biases that may skew public discourse and lack the legitimacy of institutions like universities, which are built to shield researchers from major conflicts of interest. 

The exodus of talent from many universities is partially outside of their hands. Federal and state lawmakers often control the resources available to public institutions. They have yet to equip universities with the resources and tools required to assist with navigating this AI transition. In some cases, lawmakers have actively diminished support for higher education. The foreseeable result is that many professors cannot access leading AI models and many students lack AI training and literacy. These decisions have produced an academic community that is technically challenged in its ability to guide society through the myriad questions posed by AI. 

Public officials–to varying degrees and levels of specificity–flag for universities what studies, projects, and events would help meet public informational needs, but universities may not prioritize that work. For example, agencies sometimes issue requests for information–invitations for the public, especially individuals with relevant expertise–that do not result in meaningful engagement. At the federal level, agencies often receive fewer than ten comments on critical regulatory questions. More targeted outreach programs to scholars could provide agencies with more information as well as give academics a chance to share their perspectives. Relatedly, when legislative committees at the state level hold hearings on topics closely studied by a nearby university, they often opt to invite politically connected witnesses rather than professors. This preference may make for good politics but it leaves academics on the sidelines. A small amount of effort by these state actors could go a long way toward helping academics shift their research priorities. 

In this way, external actors may be partly to blame for the increasing irrelevance of higher education in AI governance conversations. But universities should also take some responsibility. Even if professors were equipped with the latest AI, some would likely fail to use it–preferring to stick to the syllabus they’ve taught from for decades and investigate the topics that they find most interesting, regardless of societal relevance. If professors persist in the belief that AI is something they can ignore and act as though they have no responsibility to monitor and contribute to the public knowledge, there’s little reason for such public funds to go toward AI tools at universities nor to improve outreach to academics to assist with AI-related questions.

Academics are not passive players in decisions to cut funds and reduce support. Across disciplines, academics have maintained incentive structures that permit many scholars to act as though it’s still 2022. In response, some academics who  appreciate the scale, speed, and societal significance of AI have left the Ivory Tower for the Silicon Tower, where the pay is higher, the tools are more sophisticated, and the culture rewards those who dive into the most important inquiries. 

Given these challenges, what can be done? This essay provides an initial call for reform, to which we hope others will also contribute. Questions of how to resolve the compensation gulf between industry and academia are left for another time. Universities–including faculty, staff, administrators, and related organizations and networks–can still make progress on establishing the conditions for increased and expedited AI research by those who opt to stay in academia. These reforms should satisfy several foundational principles, such as protecting academic freedom, creating meaningful opportunities for student participation, and addressing issues with particular importance to the university’s surrounding community. 

Again, this is a starting point. We invite academics and others to share this call for reform, add to it, and amend it; what we should not do is carry on as normal. Instead, we call for the vast majority of scholars to substantially re-orient their research, writing, teaching and service around AI. 

We think that our legislators, civil society organizations, and neighbors would be better off with  too much analysis of AI, rather than too little. We’re currently living in a world with too little analysis and it’s far from satisfactory. Not every scholar should pivot to addressing AI directly, but the majority of departments should be able to point to how their collective expertise contributes to a better societal response to this moment. A surge in focus and expenditure on AI need not last forever but is highly needed at the moment.

Recommendation #1: Identify and Prioritize Societally Important Research Questions

Professional organizations like the Association of American Law Schools (“AALS”), which represents law schools and law professors, should establish and support shared services that collect consequential questions about AI from lawmakers and AI stakeholders, such as frontier AI labs and research entities, and connect them with relevant academic communities. Staff at these organizations have extensive knowledge of the communities that exist within the discipline as well as how best to share research, advice, and engagement opportunities (as explored below). 

Additionally, participating universities can and should set up means to receive AI-related requests to provide yet another avenue for scholars to learn about how they can contribute. Imagine, for example, if universities designated a “legislative research liaison” who had the sole purpose of working with the legislature to specify their knowledge gaps. (It is worth noting that some universities already have government affairs teams that commonly interact with legislators, albeit not necessarily for this purpose.)

Of course, individuals, organizations, and governing bodies can also share their informational needs with the Ivory Tower. This need not be a costly endeavor. For instance, state legislative committees could start their next legislative session with a hearing that culminates in a research agenda that is published and sent directly to all universities. 

Recommendation #2: Enable The Necessary Resources for Timely and Thorough Research on AI

State and federal officials, as well as AI stakeholders seeking expedited expert analysis of complex questions, should ensure that participating scholars have the resources to offer valuable insights. As it stands, universities have far too few tokens, limited access to frontier models (sometimes because of their own outdated procurement standards and IT policies), and, in some cases, minimal understanding of the latest developments in AI (such as the existing and near-future capabilities of AI). 

Government officials counting on scholars to help them in their work ought to invest in their capacity to do so. AI research is not cheap. Universities are struggling to provide meaningful access to faculty, staff, and students given the high costs of many AI systems and the variability of usage-based expenses. Rather than wait for universities to procure such access, some professors are trading university roles for the lab gigs–joining labs where they know that they will be able to use the latest and greatest AI. Legislatures have yet to make the sort of sizable investments in universities required to meet the demand for AI access among experts nor to compensate experts enough to keep them on campus. In fiscal year 2025, the average state appropriation for higher education amounted to just a 2 percent increase when adjusted for inflation. 

AI labs likewise counting on scholars to assist with readying society for their transformative technology ought to lower barriers to academic investigation. While labs have offered some universities financial breaks on their tools and permitted some degree of support to researchers, there’s substantial room for improvement. Labs, including Google and Anthropic, are sitting on vast troves of user data that can inform everything from how AI may impact the labor market to the extent to which individuals are becoming reliant on AI tools for sensitive tasks. Universities could unleash their extensive interdisciplinary experts on such data if labs facilitated access. Labs may have justifiable reasons for holding that information close to the chest. In the wrong hands, data related to user habits, interests, and goals could lead to problematic outcomes. That said, Anthropic, OpenAI, and others cannot at once stress their concern about society’s readiness for transformative AI while keeping the information necessary to assist with that effort locked away. 

Recommendation #3: Reward Contributions to Societally Relevant Work on AI

Academics may be hesitant to alter their research agenda and planned publication goals if doing so is likely to block professional progress. Tenure requirements are often tied to adherence to the existing, protracted processes. What’s more, even those requirements are completed on paper–i.e. publication of a certain number of articles, tenure decisions are commonly shaped by norms and biases that further obligate applicants to invest in the status quo. For example, in the discipline of economics, tenure may be especially likely to be awarded if the applicant has published in one of five journals. 

Alternative contributions to the discipline, especially those done in response to demand for input on AI questions, should clearly and meaningfully inform tenure, compensation, professional recognition, and perhaps university obligations, such as committee assignments. In addition to rewarding traditional research, universities eager to meet this AI moment should formalize recognition of the following: 

  • public engagement research (albeit likely in a truncated form and via more accessible outlets),
  • advice (testifying before legislative bodies, responding directly to government requests for information and the equivalent from labs), and 
  • engagement (meeting with legislators, regulators, and AI company policy staff, teaching community courses, serving as an expert at community forums).

Accounting for these contributions to a moment of informational demand would return universities to their historical focus on knowledge creation and dissemination. Rep. Jordan Morrill, author of the eponymous act that created the nation’s land grant universities, introduced the legislation with the following vision: “Let us have such colleges as may rightfully claim the authority of teachers to announce facts, fix laws, and scatter broadcast that knowledge which will provide useful in building up a great nation.” That guiding principle informed subsequent legislation. The Hatch Act, enacted in 1887, set up “agricultural experimentation systems” at universities in each state for the purpose of:

acquiring and diffusing among the people of the United States useful and practical information on subjects connected with agriculture, and to promote scientific investigation and experiment respecting the principles and application of agricultural science.

These academic entities were expected to “conduct original research or verify experiments” related to timely agricultural questions and to produce “reports of progress . . . at least once in three months, one copy of which shall be sent to each newspaper in the states in which they are respectively located, and to such individuals actually engaged in farming as may request the same.” Notably, these reports were to be sent via the “mails of the United States” at no charge to the recipient.

Realization of Morrill’s vision and replication (with some adaptation) of the Hatch Act’s provisions in modern times would transform modern universities, many of which have serially drifted from their respective missions. 

Recommendation #4: Accelerate Publication and Delivery to Stakeholders

Academic research tends to move at the speed of their respective research journals, which are rarely known for their haste. As of 2013, the publication cycle–from submission to public distribution–in business and economic journals often took 18 months; physics, comparatively moving at hyper-speed, averaged 9 months for that cycle. While some degree of delay is unquestionably necessary to probe and refine research, many scholars would conclude that the time between paper submission and publication could be shortened with minimal or, given the speed of AI, perhaps even justifiable losses to quality. 

Rather than tolerate continued reliance on those processes, domains should identify suitable alternatives that may allow for sufficient review while not unnecessarily delaying release. While many pre-print avenues exist, such as ArXiv and SSRN, it may nevertheless still be the case that the existing norms around length and formatting standards still slow a scholar’s dissemination of information that may be especially valuable to AI stakeholders. For example, it may be the case that in certain scenarios the most valuable thing to state or federal officials is a wide-range of white papers or even two-page memos from a range of practitioners. Such memos would substantially depart from the traditional research paper in just about every domain yet have an incredible impact on a pressing policy matter. 

Minimally, disciplines should commit to making their research outputs open source when possible. Academic research that lives behind a paywall will inevitably fall short of its potential to contribute to public discourse. Yet, in many disciplines only a fraction of articles are open source. Theoretically, authors of paywalled pieces may share shorter, more accessible versions through alternative means. Still, it’s antithetical to the mission of universities–especially public universities–to impose gates on knowledge. The need for open knowledge is all the greater with respect to research that addresses timely matters, such as AI. Furthermore, the materials, data, and analysis code underlying empirical research (when relevant) should be made publicly available and be as transparent as possible. By adhering to this principle of open science, empirical fields can move faster, providing opportunities to ascertain which findings are reproducible and replicable more quickly.

Conclusion 

Universities have obligations to help support the societies in which they are embedded. Novel problems and possibilities presented by this AI moment undoubtedly call for substantial assistance from our educational institutions. The call has not been answered. In fact, many of the individuals best suited to assist universities at this time of public need are leaving. The public ought to demand more–from universities, from state and federal government officials, and from AI labs. 

Universities can and should change their priorities and practices to better serve their external stakeholders. Different universities will adopt different approaches. Some will be more successful than others. This letter is meant to spark conversations that lead to tangible reforms,, not to advance a single best approach. Each discipline and institution may have varied answers but we think they all ought to center on a contemporary version of what Walter Murray, first president of the University of Saskatchewan, wrote in 1908: 

What is the sphere of the university? Its watchword is service—service of the state in the things that make for happiness and virtue as well as the things that make for wealth. No form of that service is too mean or too exalted for the university. It is as fitting for the university, through correspondence classes, extension courses, supervision of farmers’ clubs, traveling libraries, women’s institutes or musical tests to place within the reach of the solitary student, the distant townsman, the farmer in his hours of leisure or the mothers and daughters in the home the opportunities for adding to their stores of knowledge and enjoyment, as it is that the university should foster researches into the properties of radium or the causes and cure of swamp fever.

It is an obligation for universities to serve the public. The need is especially high in this time of drastic technological change, with AI adoption happening faster than the adoption of any other technology in human history. We hope universities will embrace the recommendations in this essay, responding more effectively to the AI moment.

items.title: Microsoft Defender Now Supports Linux Desktops

"Starting today, Linux desktops are now officially supported by Microsoft Defender," reports Neowin. The offering includes antivirus protection, endpoint detection and response, vulnerability management, threat hunting, and device isolation. From the report: Microsoft is also making it easier to onboard desktops through streamlined methods, offering a unified security operations experience, strengthened security, and improved response times. Organizations that are already familiar with securing Linux servers via Defender should feel right at home securing desktops too, as the experience is exactly the same. That said, you do need Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 or a Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 subscription. You can enroll Defender on workstations using the same deployment methods you use for servers, but do check out the prerequisites here.

items.title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it.

French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire.

The hacks that didn't have to happen

Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores.

items.title: ICE’s Lies About A Man Officer Ran Over Undone By Footage Captured By Nearby CCTV Camera
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
Here’s something ICE pretends has happened:

ICE alleged in a statement that “Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

ABC13 reached out to an ICE spokesperson, who said agents were attempting to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who was their intended target.

ICE alleges Mendoza-Cervantes entered the United States illegally from Mexico five times and had a final order of removal issued by a judge. The agency also alleges Parra-Hernandez is in the country illegally.

Now, if you’re an absolute prick (or an ICE officer, but I repeat myself), you may think this lie is technically correct. After all, Miguel Parra-Hernandez was struck by the front of an ICE vehicle while running through a parking lot. So, he was running in front of an ICE vehicle when things happened that ICE attributes to nobody (“was struck”).

But the verbal tense means everything here. If all you saw or heard was the ICE statement, you would assume the man carelessly crossed a street or inadvertently stepped out into the path of an already-moving ICE vehicle.

But the proper tense here is “running” and he wasn’t initially running “in front” of an ICE vehicle. The ICE vehicle (and its unnamed driver) had to cross a street and cut through a parking lot to… um… “was struck” Parra-Hernandez.

The rest of the statement is the usual ICE bullshit meant to fool idiots into believing whatever happens to migrants is their own fault, as though being in the country illegally should be met with something that looks a lot like attempted vehicular manslaughter. That the person ICE officers ran over wasn’t even the (purported) target of this arrest attempt makes this statement even stupider than it already is.

If you choose to believe ICE rather than me, feel free to watch the recording yourself. And then smack yourself around a bit for being exactly the rube this administration assumes everyone — even its voting base — to be.

What you’ll see here is Parra-Hernandez exiting a truck stopped on the street and running through a parking lot. Shortly thereafter, you’ll see the ICE vehicle accelerate from across the street and aim the accelerating vehicle directly at the running person as it enters the parking lot. While you won’t actually see the impact (due to another vehicle in the lot that seems to be part of the ICE posse), the end result was an ICE officer running over a fleeing person.

And how it happens looks very deliberate. Even if you give ICE a benefit of doubt it certainly hasn’t earned, the best case scenario is that the driver thought he could safely do some sort of pedestrian PIT maneuver or realized far too late that they wouldn’t be able to slow down in time.

But don’t bounce out the video quite yet. There’s more! An ICE officer enters the abandoned truck and parks it in the parking lot in a spot where it could easily be believed that a fleeing person would have “inadvertently” crossed paths with an ICE pursuit vehicle.

While some might speculate that ICE needed to remove the abandoned vehicle from the nearby street for public safety or whatever, the fact that it was conspicuously parked where it could shore up ICE’s narrative undercuts any assumptions of innocence on ICE’s part.

Furthermore, the vehicle was now part of an active crime scene, which meant ICE should never have moved it at all. Running someone over with a car is a crime, even if it’s accidental. An investigation needed to happen, but ICE compromised the crime scene when it absolutely didn’t need to, even if its intentions (allow traffic to flow) were pure. There were plenty of ICE officers on the scene that could have directed traffic until the locals showed up.

Given all of that, it’s 100% safe to assume the only reason the vehicle was moved was to put the truck in the path of the ICE vehicle after the fact, thus making its “ran out in front of our vehicle” narrative a bit more believable.

While there is now an independent investigation underway, it’s unlikely ICE will cooperate in any way. And it’s probably only a matter of time before the feds step in and sweep this under a rug that cannot possibly have any more room for additional cover-ups. At least the local prosecutor and sheriff’s office seem interested in digging into this, rather than just run interference for Trump’s anti-migrant efforts.

On Saturday, Harris County Attorney Abbie Kamin issued a statement regarding the incident, stating in part:

“Time is of the essence in getting the facts, and the public deserves clear, accurate answers.

ICE must cooperate fully with the local investigation. My office supports Sheriff Ed Gonzalez and District Attorney Sean Teare in their ongoing independent investigation, and the Harris County Attorney’s Office stands ready to assist and support these critical efforts. We will continue to monitor developments closely as the facts become clear.

Let’s raise a glass to the undertrained, overly aggressive officers of ICE. They can’t get away with much because they’re too stupid and aggro to realize there are cameras everywhere these days. And even if they can’t be bothered to wear/activate the mandated body cams ICE has been dragging its feet about since late last year, someone or something else is bound to catch them in the act. But until we get a few convictions nailed down, the entire administration will remain the embodiment of Trump’s “I could shoot someone on Fifth Ave. and get away with it” (lightly paraphrased, you MAGA pedants) boast.

items.title: US Tech Giants Warn Europe That Data Sovereignty Requirements Could Cost $128 Billion
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A study commissioned by CCIA Europe, whose members include Amazon, Google, and Meta, estimates that the EU's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act could impose 115 billion euros ($128 billion) in costs over a decade as governments and companies migrate workloads and rewrite software. The figure is more than six times the European Commission's upper estimate. However, roughly 80 billion euros ($89 billion) of it comes from a modeled scenario assuming sovereignty rules are extended to 25% of cloud workloads in essential private-sector industries.The Register reports: The report specifically targets Article 31 of the proposed legislation, which it says could allow the Commission to extend sovereignty requirements into essential private-sector services. CCIA argues that forcing businesses to move away from existing cloud infrastructure could trigger expensive software redevelopment projects, with code rewriting and re-architecting accounting for 69 percent of its estimated costs. Luxembourg would apparently take the biggest hit, with the study putting the cost at 1,711 euros per worker over ten years. Denmark (905 euros), Austria (900 euros), and Finland (864 euros) also face hefty bills, as does Ireland (856 euros), which hosts the European headquarters of several US tech giants. CCIA is urging EU governments to overhaul the proposed legislation, limit sovereignty restrictions to sensitive workloads, and abandon requirements based on corporate origin or personnel nationality in favor of what it calls risk-based technical safeguards. "Member States cannot rely on the Commission's incomplete estimates when deciding CADA's strict sovereignty requirements for cloud and AI providers," said Mitchell Rutledge, CCIA Europe's policy manager. "Taxpayers and businesses will foot the bill, yet the official assessment missed 70 percent of CADA's true impact." For AWS and Google, offering European customers greater control over their data also helps retain business that might otherwise migrate to European competitors. It's a rather convenient arrangement: sell customers sovereignty on one hand, while an industry association representing your interests warns governments against imposing too much of it on the other.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Google Is Silently Linking Your Phone Number Across All Signed-In Accounts
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Google has made Android's phone-number verification opt-out, automatically verifying and associating a device's phone number with every Google account signed in on that phone, including secondary and work accounts. Android Authority reports: As spotted in a recent Reddit thread, users report receiving confirmation emails out of the blue from "noreply-phone-verification@google.com" stating that their phone number has been verified. The feature, known in Google settings as "Phone number verification," links your active phone number across all Google accounts signed in on the same phone, including secondary profiles, work accounts, and throwaway handles. Google's support documentation has long noted that it periodically re-verifies your device's phone number to keep communication and recovery features up to date. However, this support page was updated sometime between August and October 2025 to add this rather aggressive behavior of turning on phone number verification by default, as well as adding all phone numbers to all Google accounts signed in on the device. To disable automatic phone number verification on Android, open your phone's Settings app, tap Google, and select the All Services tab. Under Privacy & Security, find Phone number verification and turn off Verify phone numbers automatically. "[T]urning off the phone number verification toggle only prevents future linking," notes the report. "If Google has already attached your number across secondary accounts, you will need to open your Google Account Personal Info page, head to Contact info > Phone, and manually remove the number from each profile where it doesn't belong." Is this conversation helpful so far?

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: MAGA Built The Censorship Machine It Spent Years Falsely Accusing Democrats Of Building
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
This is not a unique or new observation, but so many MAGA attacks on others are projection, claiming that Democrats were doing the very things that MAGA always knew they would do if they were in charge. We’ve certainly spent plenty of time talking about Donald Trump’s myriad and non-stop attacks on free speech, and just recently I wrote about how Trump has turned his FCC into the very “ministry of truth” that Fox News falsely claimed Biden had created. But two recent articles show how MAGA has gone all in on doing the two things it most loudly (and falsely) accused the other side of: suppressing free speech on campus, and running a “censorship industrial complex” to coerce private companies into silencing speech it doesn’t like.

On the “free speech on campus” thing, we already know that the Trump admin has disappeared students for their speech. But Adam Serwer, over at The Atlantic, has an incredible story on how MAGA officials in Texas have effectively silenced all kinds of speech across universities in Texas.

At Texas Tech, medical students no longer learn about racial disparities in medical care. Faculty at the university’s medical center in Lubbock were advised to “refrain from treating transgender patients, for any medical condition, if a medical student was present,” according to a lawsuit filed by the American Association of University Professors. (When asked for comment, a spokesperson said that the university’s “written guidance is publicly available and expressly protects instruction necessary for licensure and patient care.”) According to the same lawsuit, the censorship bot—officially known as the Course Content Review Process—ordered a Tech philosophy professor to remove Plato’s Republic from a syllabus because “it references Plato’s beliefs concerning gender roles and homosexuality.”

Professors in the Texas A&M system have had to strip their syllabi too. According to an ACLU lawsuit, last January, Aaron George, a professor at Tarleton State University, was told by administrators to remove A Gay Manifesto, a Stonewall-era LGBTQ-rights pamphlet, and White Flight, a history of urban segregation, from his American-political-history course. After a student complained that a different class the professor taught violated university policy, George was informed by administrators that it would be canceled if he did not make “necessary” (but unspecified) changes. He cut a reference in the course description to the significance of the Fourteenth Amendment for LGBTQ rights, and the class was allowed to proceed.

The University of Texas at Austin, the flagship school of the UT system, announced last month that it was eliminating majors in Africana studies, Mexican American and Latino studies, women’s and gender studies, and race and migration studies. More than 100 courses have been flagged for removal from the core curriculum, primarily ones relating to slavery, race, gender, sexuality, and the environment. Consolidating majors isn’t necessarily nefarious, nor is rethinking a core curriculum (a central group of courses from which students must take a certain number to graduate). But these changes are happening, Lauren Gutterman, an American studies professor at UT, told me, “entirely because of the political context.”

Where are all the folks who spent years screaming about “academic freedom” and insisting that colleges were censoring conservative speech? Remember how Bari Weiss and Joe Lonsdale created their “University of Austin” because (they falsely claimed) there were no universities where people could speak freely — and then they fired someone for suggesting that there might be some value in thinking about the importance of diversity.

Hilariously, Texas Governor Greg Abbott had signed a bill back in 2019 guaranteeing “free speech on campus.” But as Serwer’s piece details, these days there are all sorts of banned topics on Texas college campuses, and basically none of free speech grifters who spent years crying crocodile tears over supposed attacks on “campus speech” seem to have anything to say about it.

Even more ridiculous, Serwer details how Texas Tech is using AI to scan syllabi for wrongthink, with predictably stupid results:

Alan Barenberg, a history professor who specializes in the Soviet Union, was told to remove readings by the Princeton historian Joan Scott and the French philosopher Michel Foucault from his Ph.D.-level historiography class, after they were flagged by the AI—whose assessments he described to me as “completely inaccurate.” It also seemed to have mixed his course up with a different one. The texts were part of a unit of the class related to how treatment of gender in historical research has changed over time. “These things have been taught in classes for a long time,” Barenberg told me. The material is controversial, he said, only “in the eyes of a few people who aren’t even actually on campus.”

“The fact that the system AI doesn’t work, that it makes inaccurate pronouncements—that’s a feature, not a bug. They don’t care if it’s accurate or not. They just want to be able to say, Look, we’re making sure that your children are not being exposed to these horrible ideas from these radical professors,” Barenberg said. “A key part of how authoritarian systems often work is that, through the vagueness and sending up signals and vibes, they’re essentially saying, You know what not to do, but being deliberately vague about it.”

Although the AI is now reviewing only some courses, the university could extend the process to more.  For now, professors are the ones responsible for volunteering whether their own materials may be considered controversial. Many, unsure of what might trigger the bot, told me that they had private conversations with administrators who told them to simply self-censor and remove materials from their courses in advance, so as not to draw the wrath of leadership or lawmakers.

So the “free speech on campus” crowd is now actively censoring speech on campus because a computer program told them it was woke. What could go wrong?

Now, the other story: Anthony Fisher, at MS Now, is pointing out how Donald Trump has absolutely created the “censorship industrial complex” that a bunch of factually challenged “free speech” grifters insisted the Biden admin had built.

MAGA-adjacent journalists, one of whom now runs CBS News, have claimed there was a vast “censorship industrial complex” — run exclusively by Democrats, of course. In 2022, they peddled Elon Musk’s nothingburger “Twitter Files” as the free speech scandal of the century. It was, in fact, a fake controversy driven by politically motivated reasoning and faux-journalistic laziness, and none of them ever had the integrity to admit they were led by the nose by the world’s richest man or that they got the story completely wrong.

But the Trump Censorship Industrial Complex is very real. It is chilling speech in the media, academia and everyday life.

“Over the last two years, there’s been escalating threats against ABC,” Wilkinson said in court Tuesday. She added that the president “has control over vast regulatory powers that he’s willing to use against those he does not like” and “has put in place a chairman at the FCC who understands his marching orders and is not shy about saying so. These are blatant violations of the U.S. Constitution.”

You can follow the links there to get more details, but the most important detail is that when some individuals and two MAGA-run states sued the Biden admin over the supposed “censorship industrial complex,” it was two Trump-appointed Supreme Court Justices — Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — who pointed out how wrong they were.

During oral arguments Kavanaugh practically laughed at the lawyer making these claims, pointing out that government officials merely pressing their side of the story with no associated threats or coercion happens every damn day in the government, and is not even remotely close to censorship. Then Coney Barrett wrote the decision of the court, noting the complete lack of evidence tying any government outreach to actual moderation decisions, and called the lower court judge’s factual findings “clearly erroneous.” That resulted in the case being sent back for lack of standing due to the fact that there was zero evidence presented of any coercive behavior.

So there was no Biden “censorship industrial complex,” but there absolutely is a Trump one. As Fisher notes:

The Trump administration’s juvenile bullying has already restricted The Associated Press’ White House access for more than a year over its refusal to call the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. And those efforts have now bled over into MAGA Republican-dominated states, like Alabama, where a new law requires “all state and local entities and their employees” to refer to the body of water as the Gulf of America. That means public schools, colleges and even the state’s NPR affiliate have to abide by Trump’s embarrassing attempt at patriotic virtue signaling.

Carr has threatened broadcasters’ licenses for reporting accurately on Trump’s asinine and failing war on Iran. The administration is still in a legal battle with MS NOW, CNN and Politico, as it preposterously claims its ban on the three news organizations is a national security issue. And the administration has been siccing its secret police force on private citizens who’ve written social media posts criticizing Immigrations and Customs Enforcement’s brutal crackdown on immigrants — and U.S. citizens caught in their lawless dragnets.

And not a peep from those who falsely argued that it existed under Biden. How strange.

Once again, those complaints were all lies and projection. Richard Hanania, the far right commentator who spent years spreading hate and white supremacy online and now pretends to have turned against the very MAGA Trumpism he long supported, at least admitted clearly, back before Elon Musk took over Twitter, that right wingers like himself only scream about “censorship” because they want to do it themselves. This was in response to him getting banned from (again, pre-Elon) Twitter for violating its rules against hateful conduct. At the time, he said:

I don’t feel particularly oppressed by leftists. They give me a lot more free speech than I would give them if the tables were turned. If I owned Twitter, I wouldn’t let feminists, trans activists, or socialists post. Why should I? They’re wrong about everything and bad for society. Twitter is a company that is overwhelmingly liberal, and I’m actually impressed they let me get away with the things I’ve been saying for this long.

But that kind of honesty about how much MAGA authoritarians want to censor people while screaming about non-existent “censorship” from the other side is rare.

Still, it would be nice if everyone stopped pretending that Greg Abbott, Donald Trump, or Elon Musk ever stood for free speech at all. They all whined about free speech solely as a means to make sure that they were in charge of censoring those they disliked.

items.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Self-Replicate Through IoT Devices
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that's capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that "a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there's no centralized point to shut off -- though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own." Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into "shards" running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output. [...] This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai, install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it. "Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload." Further reading: Anthropic Bans Cruelty Toward Claude

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Google Play Now Lets Anyone Build Private, Vibe-Coded Apps That Run On Android
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Google Play is adding support for private personal Android apps, allowing users to build an app with tools like Google AI Studio and run it on their own devices without publishing it publicly to the Play Store. "These personal apps won't show up in Google Play's search or listing pages, and won't be shared with anyone except for the app's creator," reports TechCrunch. From the report: The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store's some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play's existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child's T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. items.title: Court Filings Show DHS Is Collecting Info On Protesters, Feeding It To Palantir
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
More evidence is piling up that contradicts the almost-but-not-quite denials given by administration officials in response to allegations about the DHS compiling a database to keep tabs on protesters.

Just a few months ago, “Immigration Czar” Todd Lyons was trying to turn credible accusations into a nothingburger by deploying a few vague and trite statements that didn’t actually add up to real denial. Protesters were reporting that immigration officers were taking photos of protesters, trying to gather other identifying info from them when accosting them, and then doing truly nasty stuff plainly meant to deter them from engaging in further protests or simply trying to document what ICE officers were doing out in the field.

Protesters and observers who have encountered ICE officers have reported multiple drive-bys by ICE officers at their personal homes, calls from unidentified officers containing veiled threats of punishment, and other forms of intimidation that are reliant on having enough collected data to locate people’s homes, phone numbers, places of business, etc.

If this database of protesters and other ICE opponents doesn’t actually exist, it would seem unlikely that any immigration officer would refer to it. But that has happened and that’s what drew the questions from congressional reps that Lyons then attempted to dance around.

Rep. Lou Correa, D-Calif., cited a well-circulated clip of an ICE agent in Portland, Maine, telling a person videotaping that she would be added to a “nice little database.” 

“I can’t speak for that individual,” said Todd Lyons, who serves as acting director of ICE. “But I can assure you that there is no database that’s tracking United States citizens.”

Lyons doubled down on his denials about the database’s existence during a Senate hearing Thursday. When asked if ICE is giving protester information to any other agency, Lyons said: “We do not.” 

In his official response to congressional oversight, Lyons went a bit further… which only made things worse.

If individuals who interact with ICE officers are not arrested or detained, any information collected during those encounters is maintained consistent with applicable law and DHS and ICE policies and is treated as an official government record.

That’s the information-gathering side of things, which clearly states that ICE is collecting information on more than just the people it arrests. And since it’s collecting this information on non-arrestees in the normal course of business, the compilation is undeniably happening. Whether or not this information is segregated from the rest of the stuff ICE gathers is hardly consequential, which makes this statement from Lyons especially meaningless.

DHS is not creating or maintaining a separate, standalone database for individuals encountered that haven’t been arrested or detained.

You don’t have to create a new database. You don’t even have to silo it off. You can just dump this info in with the rest of the stuff and let those with access use this info to track down protesters in order to intimidate them.

A recent court filing in a lawsuit against the DHS brought by anti-ICE protesters in Maine (one that alleges a lot of truly troubling behavior by ICE officers) says ICE is shoving this info into Palantir’s gaping data maw, presumably to expedite future threats, intimidation, and retaliation against First Amendment-protected activity.

An explosive and newly partially unsealed court filing alleges that the US Department of Homeland Security built up dossiers on ICE observers—including their photos, license plate numbers, and other information—and stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management database, which was built by Palantir.

[…]

Plaintiffs allege in the filing, which is heavily based on documents produced by the government and depositions of DHS agents, that agents had a practice of intimidating protesters and observers. They did this, the filing says, by doing drive-bys of the observers’ homes and, in the case of at least one observer, requiring that she be referred to secondary inspection any time she tries to cross the border until at least January 2027.

The allegations are only going to get more serious the further this case proceeds. The plaintiffs are still operating with limited information, but what little they have already suggests ICE officers routinely engage in retaliatory acts against protesters and observers. From the filing [PDF]:

While the case is still in its preliminary stage, with only limited discovery, the record demonstrates that agents routinely collect images of observers’ faces and license plates, and have created retaliatory investigative records about their protected activity. Agents also threatened multiple observers with being placed on watchlists, and have continued their practice of intimidating drive-bys: in June of this year, an agent led Plaintiff Hilton to the address on her driver’s license and conspicuously stopped in front of the house. Other Mainers have experienced the same. All Plaintiffs have experienced concrete harm and have been chilled in the exercise of their First Amendment rights: Williams and Pantos have stopped all observation activity entirely, and Hilton and Fagan have reduced their protected activity or taken other precautions while doing so.

Whatever guidelines ICE may have in place (if any) to prevent ICE officers from gathering info on protesters and observers clearly isn’t working. The filing mentions multiple times where ICE officers have directly told the people they’re accosting that they would be adding them to the ICM (ICE’s case management system) or, worse, a “domestic terrorism watchlist.”

These are credible allegations, especially since some of these threats from officers have been recorded. The plaintiff who’s allegedly now facing mandatory secondary inspection at all border crossings for the next six months lends a lot of credence to claims about being added to terrorism watchlists.

DHS’s denial is hardly worth noting.

A spokesperson for DHS calls the case “meritless” and says that “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.”

All this says is that the DHS doesn’t “run” the “domestic terrorists” database. While that is true (the Terrorist Screening Dataset is overseen by the DOJ and “run” by the FBI), the Terrorist Screening Center is a multi-agency operation (including the DHS and its components) that “manages” (direct quote here) its operations. Furthermore, the DHS and its components are designated “nominators,” which means exactly what’s being denied by DHS spokespeople: officers do have the power to put people on “terrorist watchlists.”

Whether or not this lawsuit leads to more discovery, there’s no reason to give the DHS the benefit of a doubt while waiting for more information to roll in. It has already shown it’s willing to violate rights, ignore court orders, and pretend existing immigration laws don’t actually say what they say. The mass deportation machinery deployed by the Trump administration is in a state of constant acceleration. Anything that might reduce a bit of the friction — even if it’s clearly unconstitutional acts of intimidation — will be deployed until a court tells it to stop… and then for awhile after that, if recent history is any indication. And it’s all being aided by a company that’s collecting tens of millions of dollars to, basically, help ICE agents connect these dots faster.
